data.title: FTSE 100 giant to quit London for New York
data.description:
A FTSE 100 giant is quitting the London stock market for New York in a blow for the Government’s effort to stop companies fleeing the City. 

Compass, the world’s biggest catering group, will announce plans to relocate its primary stock listing from the London Stock Exchange (LSE) as early as this week, The Telegraph understands.

Compass is worth £43bn, making it among the largest 20 companies on the FTSE 100. Its exit would be the second-largest from the exchange in recent years.

Cement Roadstone Holdings (CRH), a building materials group, is the biggest firm to desert London to date, with the £54bn giant abandoning the UK in April.

Compass will join Flutter, the owner of Paddy Power and Betfair, which quit London entirely in August, blaming low levels of trading, high costs and red tape.

CRH also cited regulatory costs and poor trading for exiting the LSE in April after moving its main listing in 2023.

Ashtead, which rents out construction equipment, money-transfer specialist Wise, drugmaker Indivior and investment firm Petershill Partners have also switched their primary listings or left the LSE completely in recent years.

Compass traces its history to the foundation of two canteen operators in wartime Britain, which were merged into the catering operations of Grand Metropolitan in the late 1960s, before the business adopted the Compass name in 1984 and listed in 1988.

It comes despite a series of government reforms in the past five years aimed at reviving London’s capital markets, including the removal or lowering of barriers to UK listings, secondary fundraisings and mergers and acquisitions.

It is understood that Compass will announce plans to consult with shareholders on the move to Wall Street alongside the publication of full-year results on Tuesday, with the switch itself unlikely to happen until 2028.

Compass will also suggest that the change is motivated by its focus on opportunities in the US rather than specific concerns about the liquidity of London’s capital markets.

While the group employs more than 50,000 people in the UK and Ireland, providing meals in schools, hospitals, offices and sports stadiums, its business has become strongly biased towards North America, where it gets two-thirds of revenue and three-quarters of profit.

Compass provides food for the US army, fine dining at Wall Street banks including JPMorgan, and canteens at data centres being built in locations that lack alternative lunch options.

The company, which also has a facilities management arm, is active in 25 markets worldwide, including much of Europe and Japan, India and Australia, where it provides catering for workers in remote mining communities.

The firm plans to retain a secondary listing in London and will indicate that there is no threat to employment in the UK, The Telegraph understands.

Compass declined to comment on its listing plans, which were first reported in the Financial Times.

data.title: Anthropic lacks ‘basic moral compass’, say publishers
data.description:
Anthropic’s cavalier approach to copyright shows the AI giant “lacks a basic moral compass”, news publishers have said.

The News Media Association (NMA), which represents titles including The Telegraph, The Times and The Guardian, attacked the company after admissions in its stock market filing.

Anthropic, which went public on Thursday at a valuation of $1.5tn (£1.1tn), told investors it could not guarantee it would adhere to measures that prevented journalism from being used to train AI models.

The Claude maker said it took steps to abide by paywalls and a system known as robots.txt, which tells web crawlers what pages they can access, but that this “may not always be successful”.

Anthropic also acknowledged that it might not be able to verify whether the material it used to train its models was protected by copyright.

Theo Bamber, the chief executive of the NMA, said: “Anthropic’s IPO (initial public offering) filing confirms a chilling reality about how this new darling of the stock market operates.

“Paying for content should be a basic cost of doing business and investors should ask how long their new cash cow thinks it can go without paying its bills.

“If Anthropic’s lack of a basic moral compass does not give them pause for thought, the massive legal exposure should.”

Silicon Valley’s ‘hollow’ promises

Baroness Kidron, the crossbench peer and filmmaker who directed Bridget Jones: The Edge of Reason, said the filing showed AI companies’ promises to respect copyright were “hollow”.

She said: “The only thing that has compelled it to make this confession is the pursuit of money through its IPO. But our laws should not be a victim of their greed.”

Copyright has emerged as a major flashpoint in AI amid accusations tech companies have used vast troves of data to train their models without permission.

Dame Caroline Dinenage, the chairman of the Commons culture, media and sport committee, accused Silicon Valley firms last year of the “largest copyright heist” in history.

At the same time, the rise of chatbots and Google’s AI summaries is diverting readers away from news sites, leading to sharp drops in online traffic.

The Telegraph is among a number of British news outlets that have joined forces to stop AI giants from cashing in on their journalism.

Anthropic and rivals including ChatGPT maker OpenAI have relied on “fair use” principles under copyright law to date.

But in filings published before its stock market debut this week, Anthropic acknowledged that the legality of this approach had not been “authoritatively resolved” by courts in the US and around the world.

AI companies are facing a wave of lawsuits from publishers and rights holders about alleged copyright infringement, with The New York Times suing both OpenAI and Perplexity.

Anthropic itself was forced last year to pay $1.5bn to settle a copyright claim about its use of pirated books, with Harry Potter publisher Bloomsbury among those to receive a payout.

The filing revealed that the company faces two further lawsuits from publishers in Canada which allege their journalism was used to train Claude models.

Other outlets, including Rupert Murdoch’s News Corp and The New York Times, have opted to sign licensing deals with AI developers for the use of their content.

Anthropic acknowledged that if it could not rely on the fair use defence, it might be required to pay “significant fees” to obtain a licence.

In the UK, Labour is facing a backlash against its plans to water down copyright laws to allow AI companies to scrape data unless rights holders explicitly opt out.

Baroness Kidron added: “Anthropic is built in part on other people’s property.

“Ministers should read this filing and ask themselves who they were protecting when they refused to give creators basic transparency and whether there is any justification to refuse it now they see the abuse of our law in black and white.”

Anthropic has been contacted for comment.

data.title: What opening a joint bank account taught me about my relationship
data.description:
How do you and your partner deal with joint expenses? Let us know in the comments or email money@telegraph.co.uk*.

If you had told me a year ago that £1 doughnuts would test my relationship with my partner, I wouldn’t have believed it.

My boyfriend Alex and I have been together for two-and-a-half years, yet because work keeps us in separate cities, we have never lived together. Recently, however, we decided to take a different kind of “next step” in our relationship: opening a joint bank account.

There were practical reasons for this, but I was also curious to see how our relationship, as yet untested by more traditional milestones such as marriage, would handle an experiment such as this.

We both thought we knew each other’s attitudes to money, but creating even a relatively small shared pot compels you to turn abstract ideas about fairness, ownership and compromise into actual rules.

We agreed to put the same amount of money into the account as and when it needs topping up. Household items and food we buy when staying together are considered joint expenses, along with train tickets or petrol for travelling to see each other.

Our foray into shared finances was going swimmingly until one day, I got a notification from the bank saying that £1 had just been spent on our joint card. My partner walked in the door a few minutes later, excited because he had just found a pack of five doughnuts on sale for – you guessed it – £1.

This was something that had come up in our relationship before: Alex, a committed saver, is often content to buy or eat whatever is cheapest, while I am more of a food (and everything else) snob who would sooner spend a few extra pounds.

I wasn’t annoyed at the money, but it did puzzle me that he considered this a joint purchase when he was the only one going to be eating them. Fearful of being petty, I decided to let the issue lie.

Yet soon enough, the same question started appearing everywhere. If Alex wants the cheapest toilet paper while I would sooner spring for something softer, should he have to subsidise my preference? If we buy chocolate from the joint account but he eats most of it, is that really a shared expense?

We might have known what we were getting into. Research published by Starling Bank last year found that 76pc of surveyed couples argued about money regardless of how they managed their finances.

Becky Palmano, a 38-year-old production executive based in Jersey, faced similar issues when she first combined finances with her now-husband, Sam, also 38.

Initially, she tells me, they thought they were alike in how they approached money.

Once they began making financial decisions together, this turned out not to be the case: “My attitude is quite ‘live now’, which can occasionally become ‘spend now’, whereas Sam is more inclined to plan ahead, save and deliberate over bigger decisions like trips.”

The couple have devised a strategy for dealing with financial “missteps”, which they call “idiot tax”. The couple keep a shared savings pot of around £5,000 to cover the financial consequences of either of them doing something stupid.

“Recently, I booked Sam on to entirely the wrong flight. Idiot tax,” says Palmano. “The basic rule is that if it’s a genuine mistake, you’re allowed to be annoyed, but you don’t get to turn it into a huge argument about the money. Whoever has messed up has to hold their hands up, admit they’ve been an idiot and, ideally, not do it again.”

She also spoke of an incident early on in their relationship where a disastrous weekend away resulted in a series of costly financial blunders, including a last-minute hire car (which then got damaged) and a speeding fine.

Ultimately, they decided to split the damage 50-50 after realising that sometimes, trying to establish exactly whose expense something is “becomes more ridiculous than the expense itself”.

This was a trap I had already fallen into with my partner. After an absurd discussion where we tried to calculate who was subsidising more of the other’s spending, we resolved to continue splitting things equally and save ourselves the trouble of accounting for every difference in consumption and salary.

Admittedly, this isn’t something I usually agree with. I have always felt that it is best to split things equitably, so if your partner earns more than you, then what they pay in terms of rent and household expenses should reflect that gap.

Yet the difference between our salaries is small – I would estimate that Alex earns £5,000 more than me annually, although it’s difficult to know for certain as we both take on ad-hoc work.

We agreed that for the time being, our relationship would be best served by letting the little things go.

Tom Desborough, a financial planner at Paradigm Norton, suggests that those with different attitudes to spending are not inherently incompatible. He finds most couples are willing to compromise a bit because it’s part of being in a loving relationship.

If you want to avoid being blindsided by your partner’s spending habits, however, he recommends asking more holistic questions early on in the relationship. For example, where do you see your life in 10 or 20 years’ time, or if you won the lottery, what would you do?

You may already know that you are both savers, but what you are saving your money for is just as important.

Desborough also recommends a “yours, mine and ours” approach, rather than pooling everything. It is a system Eduardo Gomes, 38, and his wife Carla, 44, eventually arrived at, although it took an expensive accidental purchase to get them there.

When they moved from Brazil to London, they combined their finances to cover rent and household costs, using a single credit card.

During Covid, Eduardo found an auction website and placed bids on five coffee machines, unexpectedly winning all five at a cost of around £1,000. Understandably, his wife wasn’t pleased. He managed to sell four of the machines for a profit, but they have since switched to having both joint and separate accounts.

Now, Gomes says, they have learned from each other’s attitudes; Carla has taught him the importance of having a savings buffer, especially as she now works part-time to spend more time with their young daughter, and he has encouraged her to be more adventurous.

“Ultimately, we complement each other’s spending behaviours,” he says.

This was another lesson Alex and I learned. We could have gone back and forth for hours over whose attitude to money was better, but ultimately, if we wanted to move forward, we needed to accept that there wasn’t going to be an outcome where either of us “wins”.

In that sense, combining even a small part of our finances became a useful trial run for the long-term relationship we hope to have. We might have spent ages debating fairness and compromise in the abstract, but we needed to put those ideas into practice to see how we would build a financial life together.

Of course, compromising over £1 doughnuts is one thing. Making bigger decisions down the line will be considerably harder. The important thing is that we understand each other’s respective money attitudes before we try.

data.title: Grid operator handed £1bn Treasury loan to meet soaring wasted wind costs
data.description:
Britain’s grid operator has been forced to seek a £1bn loan from the Treasury to meet soaring wasted wind payments.

The National Energy System Operator (Neso), the body responsible for keeping the lights on, has been granted extra taxpayer support after the bill for so-called balancing costs hit £2bn this year.

That is up from £1.5bn in 2025. Neso has to commit ever-growing amounts to pay wind farms to switch off when the grid cannot cope with their output.

This is alongside payments to gas-fired power stations to replace lost power.

Neso confirmed its request for extra cash on Thursday, saying it had struck a “time-limited extension of a working capital facility from £700m to £1.7bn”.

It comes after the windy autumn weather pushed up balancing costs to £740m in October alone.

Typically, Neso recoups this money from energy bills. But balancing costs are now rising more quickly than the grid operator can recover the cash.

Wind farms are typically shut off because of transmission bottlenecks on the wires connecting Scottish turbines with households south of the border.

The low capacity of those transmission lines means excessive power can cause overheating, forcing turbines to be deactivated to avoid damage when it is too windy. Wind farm operators are then compensated as a result.

However, the main costs are incurred in paying gas-fired stations in southern England to fire up to compensate for the missing wind power.

This is always expensive but is currently made worse by the surge in gas prices caused by the Iran war.

The normal wholesale price of power is around £170 per megawatt hour, but Neso has been forced to pay significantly more over the past three months.

The Telegraph revealed earlier this month that Neso was paying around £1,500 per megawatt hour to at least three power stations.

‘Labour’s obsession with net zero’

Kathryn Porter, an analyst, said the costs had also been amplified by Neso’s failures to forecast supply and demand accurately.

She said: “The scale of the forecasting failure is extraordinary. Neso knows about transmission constraints and has forecasts of wind output and demand well before delivery.

“Where substantial wind curtailment is inevitable, arranging it in advance would allow wholesale prices to reflect the electricity that can actually be delivered.”

Balancing costs are common, but they have spiralled in the UK because so many wind farms were built in rural areas where there is not enough grid capacity to carry their output.

Greg Jackson, the chief executive of Octopus Energy, said: “This is yet another symptom of the failure to reform the electricity market, and it all falls on energy users at a time we’re already paying eye-watering prices.”

Richard Tice, Reform UK’s energy spokesman, said Labour’s focus on renewables such as wind power was exposing households and businesses to ever-greater costs.

He said: “Grid operator Neso has to borrow £1bn more from Treasury to keep the lights on by paying double: compensating wind farms not to turn off and begging gas generators to turn on.

“This is entirely due to Labour’s obsession with net zero that is making everyone poorer and killing jobs.”

Neso said the Treasury loan did not reflect the organisation’s underlying financial position.

A spokesman said: “We have agreed an extension to our working capital arrangements, allowing current balancing tariffs to remain unchanged and providing predictability for suppliers and their customers for the remainder of the charging year.”

John Constable, of the Renewable Energy Foundation, said: “Neso is having to borrow to pay a constraint bill that has spiralled because successive governments connected wind farms far faster than the grid needed to carry their output.

“The only lasting reform is to stop compensating wind generators for constraints they could have foreseen, so that the cost falls on developers rather than on bill payers and now taxpayers.”

data.title: London house prices suffer worst drop since financial crisis
data.description:
Property prices in inner London have suffered the worst drop since the financial crisis as higher mortgage rates slow the capital’s housing market.

A toxic cocktail of soaring borrowing costs, high levels of stamp duty and the looming mansion tax caused central London property prices to slump 7.2pc in the 12 months to September, according to figures from the Office for National Statistics (ONS).

It means the average price of a home in inner London’s 12 boroughs and the City – which includes areas such as Camden, Tower Hamlets, Newham and Lambeth – dropped by just over £48,000 in a year, falling from £669,532 to £621,491.

However, the data revealed there was a significant divide in the areas of the capital where property prices fell. Outer London boroughs recorded just a 0.1pc decline in the price of a home in the 12 months to September.

On average, property prices across the capital dropped 3.5pc in the year to September.

Jonathan Hopper, the chief executive of Garrington Property Finders, said: “This huge divergence reflects the gulf between the buyers typically drawn to the two areas. Demand in outer London comes largely from domestic buyers, and while this has softened over the past year, it has been resilient.”

He warned that in stark contrast “a series of punitive tax increases”, including the looming mansion tax, had dented demand in inner London, with wealthy, international buyers reconsidering whether to purchase property.

Despite the slump, official figures showed that average UK house prices increased by 1.2pc, to £273,000.

London and the South East were the only two regions in the UK to record a drop in annual house prices, the data from the ONS showed.

The capital will be the hardest hit by Labour’s upcoming mansion tax, also known as the high-value property surcharge. The levy will hit properties worth £2m or more with a surcharge of at least £2,500 a year when it comes into effect in April 2028.

Wealthy areas of inner London have also recorded double-digit declines in annual property prices as they grapple with the effect of the scrapping of non-dom status and higher stamp duty rates.

House prices in Kensington and Chelsea declined 15.6pc year on year to an average of £1.17m in September 2026, down from £1.39m, according to Land Registry data.

In Westminster, house prices dropped 18.5pc in the year to September, with the average property costing £861,130, compared to £1.06m in September 2025.

Inner London’s flat market has also experience a significant slowdown, as average flat prices dropped 8.5pc. This compared with a 2.6pc decline in the price of detached properties over the same period.

Despite the fall in property prices in the capital, prospective buyers will still feel the squeeze, as borrowing costs have risen sharply since the outbreak of the Iran war, adding hundreds to mortgage repayments.

Paige Tao, an economist at PwC UK, said: “First time buyers entering the market with smaller deposits are more exposed to higher mortgage rates, while those who have moved out of their childhood home face the added challenge of saving for a deposit.”

data.title: ‘Saks f---ed with my mum’: The millionaire on a mission to take down store giant
data.description:
A millionaire is paying protesters to picket a luxury New York department store that he claims fired his mother after a customer attacked her.

Jeffrey Vinokur, 36, said the daily protests outside Saks Fifth Avenue would go on “for as long as it takes” until justice was served.

He is demanding that the company’s chief executive apologise publicly and an outside investigation be launched and has also called on New York to change its employment laws to protect workers who are victims of crime.

The protests started last Thursday – just before Saks’s busiest season – with women holding signs saying: “BEATEN AT SAKS. THEN FIRED. I WANT ANSWERS.”

Mr Vinokur, an entrepreneur who sold his education-tech company for $100m (£79m) last year, doubled the number of picketers this week from 15 to 30 to increase pressure on the company.

“I can go on for years – that’s what scares Saks the most,” Mr Vinokur told The Telegraph. “They’re not going to get away with it.”

Saks, once an icon of American luxury, has in recent years been plagued by falling sales and financial woes that led to Saks Global’s bankruptcy filing in January and subsequent restructuring. Its prestige, in turn, has suffered.

Laza Susuni, Mr Vinokur’s 62-year-old mother, had been a new sales associate at its 10-floor flagship store in Midtown Manhattan when she reported being attacked on June 28.

The incident began with a customer asking Ms Susuni where to find a fashion brand. When Ms Susuni asked the price point, she claimed the customer became enraged and demanded she be instantly fired.

A verbal dispute followed. The customer allegedly then began harassing and recording Ms Susuni in a dressing room area, where her manager had instructed her to wait while she spoke with the customer.

The situation escalated when Ms Susuni also took her phone out to record.

According to Ms Susuni’s police report, the customer then punched her in the face with a closed fist and kicked her in the stomach.

A photograph showed her being taken to hospital in an ambulance with minor injuries.

The customer was arrested and charged with five counts of assault and harassment, according to police and court documents. She pleaded guilty to a misdemeanour and was released.

Five days after the incident, Ms Susuni was fired by Saks.

“I was betrayed by the company. It was just horrific,” she told The Telegraph. “My safety, dignity and wellbeing was violated… But there was no justice for me being attacked.”

In her termination letter, seen by The Telegraph, Saks wrote that the decision was a “result of serious policy violations and insubordinate behaviour”, citing her using her phone to record.

“Your lack of judgment and inappropriate conduct directly escalated a situation with a customer and resulted in a physical altercation, and endangered the safety of yourself and others,” the letter read.

Mr Vinokur accused Saks – which is managed by Exemplar Luxury Group, a holding company which also owns luxury department stores Bergdorf Goodman and Neiman Marcus – of treating his mother as a “disposable minimum-wage worker”.

He cast it as a David versus Goliath battle. “It’s kind of like, but not exactly, rich versus poor. But it turns out the poor actually fight back,” he said.

Mr Vinokur has also published a dossier of evidence – “the Saks Files” – related to five other cases in which Saks’s employees alleged they were harassed, assaulted, or sexually assaulted and then fired or forced to leave.

It details lawsuits between 1994 and 2024. Most were settled out of court.

Mr Vinokur said the evidence suggested a “horrifying pattern”.

“I don’t want money. I want answers,” he wrote on his new website. “Saks pays women for confidentiality. I’m paying women to stand outside Saks Fifth Avenue every single day until they answer for this.”

A spokesman for Saks said: “We take matters of employee and customer safety and security extremely seriously.

“It is the company’s firmly held policy that we do not retaliate against any employee who reports violations of our policies or the law. All reports are investigated promptly and thoroughly.”

Mr Vinokur claimed that Saks’s legal team was pleading with him to stand his growing number of protesters down, but he has no such plans.

“That’s not my kind of personality. Like they f---ed with my mom,” he said.

“Saks need to be held accountable for this, and I’m going to make this law happen that’s going to protect all workers from being fired if they’re a victim of violent crime.”

Most states, New York included, do not have a law prohibiting termination because an employee was a crime victim. Only 25 states have mandated leave for employees who are victims of violent crimes.

Mr Vinokur said he had the time and money to continue the demonstration.

Come rain or shine, he said he would be outside Saks with his mother, other family members and the for-hire protesters. “What I was really touched by is the number of these women… who said: ‘When I read about this, it made me mad. That’s why I took this job’,” he said.

On Tuesday, Mr Vinokur extended the protests outside Bergdorf Goodman, Saks’s sister retailer. Next Monday, he said he had hired 90 protesters to disrupt Saks’s Christmas light show.

The department store sits across Fifth Avenue from the Rockefeller Centre Christmas tree – New York’s focus of festivities and a magnet for shoppers and visitors during peak holiday times.

Mr Vinokur said: “My audience is [the equivalent size of] Madison Square Garden Stadium every two hours. They are giving us the biggest stage in America and it’s free, no tickets.

“So I don’t want Saks to cancel the show. I want the stage.”

data.title: The West is hooked on Chinese drugs but they could save your life
data.description:
Sir Keir Starmer’s decision to invite Sir Pascal Soriot, AstraZeneca’s chief executive, to Beijing at the beginning of the year was a textbook piece of modern diplomacy.

The then-prime minister’s attempt to revive economic cooperation rested on a knockout deal that went beyond the usual warm words. Sir Pascal, a sworn Sinophile and one of the biggest cheerleaders of Chinese innovation, was only too happy to oblige.

Within hours of Sir Keir’s arrival, AstraZeneca had unveiled a plan to invest $15bn (£11bn) in China, building on its existing medical manufacturing and research capabilities in Beijing, Shanghai, Wuxi, Taizhou and Qingdao.

AstraZeneca’s pledge was the marquee announcement of Sir Keir’s trip. Sir Pascal said the “landmark investment” marked the next chapter for the company in China. For the politburo, it was further proof that their plan to turn China into a global pharmaceuticals leader has worked.

In the West, China has long been dismissed as little more than a dealer in cheap copycat medicines – both legal and illegal – and increasingly knockoffs too, such as unlicensed GLP-1 weight loss medication.

This portrayal no longer bears scrutiny, however. In recent years, the Chinese pharmaceutical industry has undergone a remarkable reinvention. Western industry leaders view it as a bona fide drug superpower at the forefront of discovery.

China controls an exciting pipeline of groundbreaking medicines and occupies a growing role as a globally important venue for clinical trials.

But for now, cooperation between East and West suits both sides. European and American drugmakers have rushed to embrace Chinese research, forging multi-billion licensing deals. Those with the appetite have opened their own labs and even set up manufacturing outposts.

Chinese science is now “the best in the world” and ignoring it is not an option, says one European pharmaceuticals chairman.

Few have led the charge as enthusiastically as Sir Pascal, AstraZeneca’s swashbuckling French boss. China is now its second-biggest market. Meanwhile GSK, the UK’s other national drug champion, has struck a series of partnerships with Chinese labs to licence promising drugs outside the country.

These relationships are critical for China’s pharmaceuticals industry, providing access to the lucrative markets that fund innovation. At home, their only customer is Xi Jinping, and he sets the price.

Yet this partnership is fragile. Amid growing concern in the US about the threat China’s new scientific prowess poses to drug supplies, innovation and even national security, industry executives fear an iron curtain will be drawn.

Drugs may be the next front in the superpower trade war that has already drawn in telecoms equipment, semiconductors, electric vehicles, rare earth minerals and solar panels.

For Europe, including Britain’s pharmaceutical giants AstraZeneca and GSK, the looming nightmare is that an American administration will sooner or later use its economic muscle to effectively outlaw their cooperation with China.

One senior figure says the possibility of a sweeping American crackdown is “probably the one question that keeps me awake at night”.

China’s rapid scientific progress

Dr Zhao Hong, a renowned Chinese cancer specialist, shocked thousands of Communist Party delegates in March last year: a Guangzhou-based biotech firm had developed a cancer drug that had outperformed the world’s bestselling equivalent in clinical trials.

The work of China’s Akeso Biopharma, lung cancer drug ivonescimab had shown that it could delay non-small-cell lung cancer progression for five months longer than US giant Merck’s Keytruda treatment – the world’s bestselling prescription drug in 2025.

The success of ivonescimab was hailed as a breakthrough moment for China’s pharmaceutical industry.

“China is at the best time of its biopharmaceutical sector’s development,” Hong told state media at the annual Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference.

The speed with which China is catching up in pharmaceuticals and biotech is astonishing.

By 2024, China had 1,255 drugs at the research stage, a nearly eight-fold jump in less than a decade. America had 1,441 – a 15pc rise – while the total in Europe had shrunk slightly to 400.

Experts attribute the leap to a fundamental shift in how the industry was perceived by the Chinese regime.

One veteran UK executive recalls how when he first used to visit China in the late 1990s, it was to complain about “counterfeits and pharmaceuticals that were really dangerous”. Today, China is seen as “a golden opportunity”, he says.

“They have moved deliberately to be at the leading edge of science,” he adds.

Beijing has provided vast support in the form of scores of state-financed biotechnology parks equipped with advanced laboratories and heavily subsidised hardware, together with a sweeping overhaul of the regulatory system beginning in 2015.

A study by Prof Yimin Cui, of Peking University, and colleagues found that the time taken to approve a drug for human trials fell to 87 days after the reforms, from 501 days previously.

Chinese researchers are helped by the sheer size of the country’s population – last counted at more than 1.4 billion – says Freddy Yip, a corporate lawyer at Cooley.

“In the US, it may take a long time to recruit sufficient patients, but in China, you have access to lots of different patients with different kinds of diseases, including many rare diseases,” Yip says.

Sir Pascal has said this combination of scientific capability and rapid execution – “China speed”, as he has called it – can help to dramatically accelerate drug development.

One of China’s leading biotech venture capitalists estimates clinical trials are “two thirds cheaper and half as quick in China”.

Progress has been spurred by a massive increase in spending on research and development – leaping from $35m in 2015 to $15bn in 2023 – and a “reverse brain drain” in which thousands of foreign-educated Chinese scientists and entrepreneurs have returned home, according to Porsche Consulting.

Chinese scientists are now at the vanguard of treatment for cardiovascular diseases and cancer, as well as spearheading drug development for metabolic conditions and neurological disorders, such as Parkinson’s, among many others.

Alarm bells in Washington

Mere months before Sir Pascal was lending heft to Sir Keir’s Beijing bridge-building mission, the Frenchman was being warmly welcomed at the Oval Office by Donald Trump.

Thanking the US president for welcoming him “in this beautiful office”, Sir Pascal was armed with another crowd-pleasing announcement: a pledge to cut drug prescription prices in the US, after Trump had accused other countries of “freeloading” at the expense of Americans.

Sir Pascal went further as well, unveiling a $50bn plan to expand the company’s existing operations in the US. In return, AstraZeneca received a three-year exemption from tariffs.

Privately, AstraZeneca executives acknowledge it was also an attempt to ward off growing concern in the White House about the deepening of ties with China.

“We are cognisant of some of the more hawkish commentary [from US politicians]. It is a delicate balancing act, and we are treading a fine line by recognising what the US is trying to achieve,” an insider says.

Yet, for all Washington’s alarm, dependency has become more pronounced, not less. Western companies have piled into the country, hoovering up clinical trial data and striking licensing deals to develop Chinese medicines outside the mainland, which they hope can then be used to treat patients across the developed world.

“This is the golden age of science and China is white-hot right now,” an industry source says.

Deal activity is being driven by anxiety among European and US companies as their pipeline of drugs peters out.

America’s biotech industry faces the alarming prospect of an estimated $350bn worth of medicines – equivalent to roughly one fifth of projected global prescription-drug revenue – losing patent protection by the end of the decade.

When patents run out, generic rivals are allowed to gatecrash the market, jeopardising sales.

Few have led the way with the verve that AstraZeneca has demonstrated.

Sir Pascal’s Beijing announcement was accompanied by a boast that it had signed 16 global licensing agreements with 15 Chinese partners since 2023 alone – thought to be the most of any overseas pharmaceuticals multi-national.

GSK hasn’t been far behind. Last year, the company struck an alliance with local giant Hengrui Pharma to develop a dozen new medicines outside the mainland. The value of the deal could eventually total $12bn.

The agreements are part of an industry-wide surge in deals totalling $138bn last year – a nearly tenfold jump since 2021 – according to data provider PharmCube. 2026 is expected to be another record.

Deal flow shows little sign of slowing.

A fortnight ago, GSK unveiled a $1.3bn pact with Hutchmed, a Hong Kong-based biopharmaceuticals company with research facilities in Shanghai, for the bulk of the licensing rights to what it called “first in-class” cancer treatments.

Brewing geopolitical storm

Amid the feeding frenzy, concern in Washington has turned to outright hostility in some quarters.

In December last year, Trump signed into law the Biosecure Act, a move widely seen as a sharp escalation in tensions and the moment the longstanding strategic rivalry between the US and China spilt into the biotechnology arena.

The act prevents US companies reliant on federal contracts and funding from working with Chinese biotech firms with ties to the Chinese military and any deemed to pose a national security risk. It also bars Chinese companies from accessing US government funding themselves.

US biotechnology companies with federal contracts are now engaged in a mad dash to purge their supply chains of equipment obtained from any Chinese biotechnology firms on the banned list.

Next up is the Biotech Investment National Security Act. Though not yet signed into law, it will subject licensing deals involving Chinese companies to national security reviews.

Though technically a screening mechanism rather than a ban on licensing Chinese drugs, it will effectively function as one, says Craig Garthwaite, a professor at Northwestern University’s Kellogg School of Management.

There is also pressure to bar the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) from accepting Chinese trial data, amid concerns about their reliability. The FDA has repeatedly rejected one of Hengrui’s cancer drugs, citing questions about quality control at its manufacturing sites.

As one senior City figure puts it: the White House has conjured up other reasons to “erect a wall around China”.

AstraZeneca’s attempt to navigate this geopolitical storm by investing in both China and the US divides opinion. Some see it as an inspired way to keep both Washington and Beijing happy at the same time.

“I think Pascal has been very smart in not allowing anybody to question his US credentials. He’s playing his cards very wisely,” the boss of a rival company says.

Others see it as a high-stakes gamble from a company that is more exposed than most of its competitors and has learnt the hard way the risks that come from operating in China.

Leon Wang, the former head of its Chinese operations, is awaiting trial on charges of illegal trading, unlawful collection of personal information and medical insurance fraud, alongside another former employee, having been arrested in 2024.

If the saga made Sir Pascal reconsider his appetite for doing business in China, there is little sign of it.

Alongside licensing deals potentially worth tens of billions of dollars, it has around 17,000 employees in China, two “global strategic” research and development centres in Beijing and Shanghai, and four advanced manufacturing sites in Wuxi, Taizhou, Qingdao and Beijing.

China is now AstraZeneca’s second-largest market after the US, accounting for roughly 12pc of the company’s global turnover, and its Chinese facilities supply more than 70 markets worldwide.

In a written submission to the Commons business and trade select committee in July, AstraZeneca described co-operation with China as a “win-win”.

But as one investor with extensive interests in China points out: “If you’re a big pharma company with a significant proportion of your licensing spend coming from China and the tap suddenly gets turned off, that’s obviously a problem.”

Europe’s wary response

Despite sharply rising tensions, there are concerns that European policymakers are still a long way off from having a coherent industrial strategy that addresses the China question.

Having been slow to react to the threat that cheap Chinese manufacturing poses to the continent’s steelmakers, solar panel producers and its car industry, the risk is that the pendulum swings too far the other way and Brussels takes a similarly antagonistic approach in trying to shut China out of other sectors, such as pharmaceuticals.

Calls by Oliver Blume, the chief executive of Volkswagen, for tougher trade measures against Beijing have been interpreted in some circles as a signal that EU-China relations are close to a tipping point after years of resistance to anti-Chinese duties from the continent’s car giants.

Yet, a senior industrialist says Europe lacks the “economic counterweight to be able to exclude China”.

“I don’t necessarily think it’s good in the long term for the US to do so, but I think it’s very dangerous for Europe,” he adds.

“We need a more nuanced industrial strategy that seeks Chinese expertise and cost effectiveness, and to somehow bring some of the economic benefit of that into Europe,” he says.

Such sentiment echoes a growing willingness among car manufacturers to partner with Chinese counterparts amid an onslaught of imports. Nissan’s decision to share its Sunderland plant with Chery, one of China’s largest car exporters, is expected to be among the first of many similar tie-ups.

Some believe the growing divide between Washington and Beijing because of pharmaceuticals may even present an opportunity for Europe.

“I’m sure Europe would be more than happy to take Chinese-developed products that are sold to them at a lower price than what they might otherwise get from the United States,” Garthwaite says.

As Brussels bureaucrats try to agree on a co-ordinated approach, the rhetoric, particularly among some influential Republicans, continues to harden.

Chris Klomp, a top lieutenant of Robert F Kennedy Jr, the US health secretary, has likened the situation to “a war”.

Anxiety has been heightened by a so-called “hot mic” incident at a Beijing military parade late last year, in which Vladimir Putin and Xi were overheard discussing the possibility that humans could live to 150 years old, thanks to advances in biotechnology.

Some China hawks saw it as further evidence that the US risked falling behind in the global race for domination in advanced science.

The Council on Foreign Relations, an influential American think tank, has called for reliance on China’s biotech know-how to be treated as a strategic vulnerability akin to critical minerals.

“The US (and just about every other nation) faces a growing risk that China will deliberately withhold essential pharmaceutical inputs as a tool of economic or political coercion … as China has done with rare-earth critical minerals,” it warned in June.

The Atlantic Council, another US think tank with a history of shaping American foreign policy, points out that the US is reliant on China for three quarters of some imported drugs and as much as 99pc of some raw materials that are critical to the production of certain key medicines.

What’s more, China’s 2020 export control law and 2021 biosecurity law “grant broad authority to weaponise pharmaceutical exports”, it said recently.

‘All in or all out’

AstraZeneca declined to comment on its position, but there are signs it is more nervous than it is willing to acknowledge.

It emerged in August that the company had held detailed discussions with American rival Bristol Myers Squibb about a potential £300bn mega-merger.

In seeking to substantially deepen its US footprint, AstraZeneca may have concluded that the best chance it has of escaping any crackdown is if the company can demonstrate it is willing to take action to address Trump’s demands for the “reshoring” of pharmaceutical manufacturing.

Radical corporate restructuring plans have also been explored in China. AstraZeneca previously looked at the possibility of carving out its Chinese business into a separate legal entity and listing it on the Shanghai stock exchange. Though nothing came of those plans, they were seen as an attempt to insulate it from mounting geopolitical tensions.

GSK, meanwhile, sees no reason for such drastic action. Publicly, all a spokesman is willing to say is that it has “a longstanding presence in China, to make sure patients can access our medicines and vaccines”.

“China is also increasingly a source of cutting-edge biopharma innovation, and we have established several important collaborations for potential new treatments in oncology, respiratory, immunology and inflammation,” the spokesman adds.

However, like AstraZeneca, it too has fallen foul of Beijing after the company was engulfed in a bribery scandal in 2014.

GSK was found guilty of bribing Chinese doctors and hospitals to prescribe its medical products and was forced to pay a record $490m fine.

That ordeal prompted GSK bosses to take a much more cautious approach in which its activities were limited to strict licensing deals rather than the asset-heavy approach of others, such as AstraZeneca.

“It [GSK] went through a very difficult time in China. The experience damaged the company immeasurably in terms of its willingness to take risks,” a City source says.

By focusing on developing local collaborations, GSK believes it can still capitalise on the opportunities in China while being “less vulnerable” than rivals who are more “asset-exposed”, an insider explains.

Yet, the same person admits it ultimately boils down to one question: “Are they [China] helping us long-term or are they harming us? And I can’t answer that, which is why we can’t afford to be all in or all out.”

Industry figures hope common sense prevails between the two superpowers.

Garthwaite acknowledges deals that come with potential national security risk should be scrutinised, while attempts to reduce American over-dependence on Chinese antibiotics are also to be applauded.

However, he says the White House needs to distinguish between drug production and drug development, which “shouldn’t be too hard”.

Another investor says patients don’t really care where the drugs come from, “as long as they’re subjected to the same trials”.

In response to a recent US ban on imports of humanoid robots, China’s foreign ministry said: “Protectionism does not make the US more competitive … it will only hurt the interests of US companies and consumers.”﻿

Yet, nor is it in China’s interests to actively undermine American science. Chinese drugmakers simply cannot afford to be shut out of Western markets, particularly the US, experts say.

“China is really vulnerable too. It has to rely on its export machine because it doesn’t have sufficient levels of internal consumption,” one analyst says.

Ultimately, industry sources admit they are at the mercy of an unpredictable Trump administration whose appetite for trade wars shows little sign of waning.

As one boardroom veteran puts it: “It’s akin to walking a tightrope – we’ll continue trying to walk it and hope we stay on.”

data.title: BT races to stop new Grand Theft Auto game crashing the internet
data.description:
BT is racing to prevent the latest instalment of Grand Theft Auto from crashing the internet as gamers rush to get a first taste of the hit title.

The telecoms giant is among the major broadband providers that have increased network capacity ahead of the rollout of the much-delayed GTA VI on Nov 19, which is expected to trigger “unprecedented” demand for data.

Several internet firms are understood to have bought more capacity from major exchanges including the London Internet Exchange (LINX) to handle the spike in traffic.

BT and other companies have also increased their use of caching – where data is temporarily stored in locations closer to the end user – limited scheduled maintenance and stepped up network monitoring.

The release of GTA VI, which is made by developer Rockstar Games, has already broken records for internet demand after fans were given a chance to pre-load the game a week ahead of its launch.

Virgin Media O2 reported its biggest-ever traffic peak and highest-ever daily data volume on Nov 10, with demand surging between midnight and 1am. LINX has recorded its highest ever traffic over the past month at 13.7 terabits per second (Tbps).

The pre-launch was also the second-biggest peak recorded across BT’s broadband network, behind only Arsenal’s Champions League semi-final clash against Atlético Madrid in May.

The eagerly-awaited release has sparked fears of congestion and disruption following similar issues during the launch of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare III in 2023.

While Rockstar has sought to limit the impact by spreading downloads of GTA VI over a week, experts warned this may not be enough to prevent disruption.

William Manzione, at network provider RETN said: “Pre-loading should help reduce the concentration of downloads on launch day, but it does not eliminate the possibility of further traffic increases.

“Players who have not preloaded the game may still download it on release day, while additional patches or updates could create another wave of demand.”

Mr Manzione said the most likely fallout would be slower downloads and localised congestion, rather than widespread outages.

Jeanie York, VMO2’s chief technology officer, said: “GTA VI has already broken broadband records before players have even entered the game, and we’re preparing for another busy day when it launches next week.

“Fans downloading in advance will spread some of that demand, but it’s too early to say whether launch day will set another record.”

A BT spokesman said: “We are building the UK’s digital backbone and connecting and protecting the country like no one else. Our networks are built to support moments of huge national demand like this.

“From the biggest gaming launches to major sporting and cultural events, BT is investing in the scale, capacity and resilience needed to keep millions of customers connected when it matters.”

GTA has been dogged by controversy since its first release in 1997 owing to the game’s graphic depiction of violence, as well as other themes including drugs, prostitution and sex.

But the game, which is largely developed by teams based in Scotland, has enjoyed runaway success. The last title in the series, GTA V, has generated more than $10bn (£7.6bn) in sales since its launch in 2013, making it the third-best-selling video game of all time.

Rockstar, which is owned by US games giant Take-Two Interactive, first unveiled plans for its sixth instalment in late 2023.

The title is rumoured to have a budget of up to $3bn, eclipsing any Hollywood movie, but has been beset by leaks and delays.

In August, Netflix agreed a deal for an exclusive early trailer of the gangland action game. The 25-minute clip racked up 31.1m views in its first four days, jumping to the top of the streaming service’s charts.

data.title: Labour’s ‘unfair’ bank tax will have consequences, warns JP Morgan boss
data.description:
The boss of JP Morgan has warned that John Healey’s bank tax raid will have consequences for Britain, as he vowed to set an “example” by finding ways to claw back the levy.

In a veiled threat to the Government, Jamie Dimon said he wanted politicians to “understand the trade-offs of these unfair penalties”.

Mr Dimon lashed out at the Chancellor after he temporarily doubled the surcharge on bank profits above £100m from 3pc to 6pc during his maiden Budget to provide “immediate support on energy bills”.

He said that any move to offset the bank tax would be “more in sorrow” than in anger, but failed to specify how he would claw back the costs, as first reported by the Financial Times.

The Wall Street banking giant expects to pay between £100m to £150m because of Mr Healey’s higher surcharge.

Mr Dimon’s latest comments will renew scrutiny of JP Morgan’s proposals for a new £3bn headquarters in Canary Wharf.

The bank has not suggested any reversal to the tower’s development but it previously stressed that the project would depend on “a continuing positive business environment in the UK”.

The latest surcharge is levied in addition to the top rate of corporation tax, which now stands at 25pc.

That means the biggest banks in Britain now face a total tax rate of 31pc – the highest level since at least 2015.

Following the Budget, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) estimated that the higher tax rate will bring in an extra £1.5bn for the Treasury.

However, it also claimed that the UK would lose roughly £190m of profits as a result of the tax rise.

Mr Dimon has been among the staunchest critics of the policy, with the bank previously claiming that it has paid £5.5bn in bank taxes since 2011.

In July, he said there would be “adverse consequences” if the Government targeted lenders with fresh windfall taxes to help fund his spending plans.

“I always thought it was wrong,” he said. “We’re a great citizen [in the UK]. We hire people there. We want to be bigger there. We train people there. We hire veterans there.

“So if a government decides to do it, there’s nothing I can do, but it will over time cause decisions made that they may not like.”

JP Morgan declined to comment.

data.title: ‘China Shock 2.0’ is crushing the West
data.description:
Robot vacuum cleaners are typically less noisy than their older, hand-operated cousins. But the volume of the Chinese-made versions is not the only quiet thing. They are also stealthily taking over the world.

Dreame, a company founded in Suzhou less than a decade ago, is now said to be the world’s biggest seller of robot vacuums. Its founder, 39-year-old Yu Hao, claims to be building a $100tn (£75tn) ecosystem of smart appliances and frontier tech.

After just two years in Britain, Dreame is still a relatively small player here. Euromonitor International put the company’s UK market share at 4pc last year.

But four Chinese companies control almost half the UK market. And their cheapest products are all priced below those of SharkNinja and Dyson, which manufacture in Asia but do at least some of the brain-work in the US and Britain, respectively.

When it comes to Chinese imports, most people think first of electric vehicles (EVs), which are swarming into markets worldwide, such as Jaecoo, a brand that has become the go-to for British consumers. It is certainly the prime battlefront, with Britain under growing pressure to mimic the EU’s tariffs of up to 45pc on EVs.

Beneath these headlines, however, cut-price Chinese imports of just about any manufactured product are now sweeping into the West and challenging local businesses.

Consumers love the low prices. But companies and governments across Europe now fear that the Chinese juggernaut will hoover up Western industries and jobs, and leave the Continent utterly dependent on the whims and will of Beijing.

The timing of this “China Shock 2.0” – the first shock was the flood of low-priced toys, clothes and other manufactured goods that hit in the early 2000s – is not a coincidence. In the past few years, Beijing has unmuzzled its most potent weapon to win the export war.

Chinese factories have long enjoyed advantages such as cheap workers and raw materials, generous subsidies and massive economies of scale. But now a new wave of cheap credit – that is, loans made on concessional or non-commercial terms – has swept through the Chinese manufacturing sector, unlocking the export tsunami.

“This is probably the single biggest component of China’s industrial policy,” says Camille Boullenois, a China expert at the Rhodium Group consultancy.

“It has been the most powerful and the most influential factor shaping the economic system in China, because the entire economic system is based on credit.”

‘Everything in China is political’

Ever since China’s banks pulled back from lending to households after the spectacular property crash of 2021, they have been scrambling to find enough borrowers.

And with the Chinese government ever more focused on ramping up high-tech and advanced manufacturing, that’s where the banks have been pouring all that surplus cash.

“There’s a natural herding in the way the Chinese private sector operates. Once everybody realised that manufacturing is where the political light was shining, then capital and human talent moved into manufacturing,” says David Lubin, of the think tank Chatham House.

The banks have become the pivotal enabler of Beijing’s ambition to ensure companies, such as Dreame, dominate global markets and supply chains.

“Lending is political, because everything in China is political. And credit is a political tool,” says Leo Austin, a businessman who advises multinationals on working in China.

These dirt-cheap loans mean that, unlike their Western rivals, many Chinese companies can receive capital on tap.

“There is always cash flow available to you, and you have no short-term fear around the viability of the business, so you can afford to be incredibly aggressive,” Austin says.

This has wrought a transformation in China that is little appreciated outside its borders.

Once there were private firms and state-owned enterprises. But now most companies are a hybrid: they have a private-sector management culture, but are almost entirely funded by government-sourced equity and state-backed lending.

Austin calls this model “state-capitalised private enterprises”. The emerging Chinese high-tech giants are almost all cut from this cloth.

Chinese banks are bound by law to lend money “in accordance with the needs of the national economic and social development, and under the guidance of the industrial policies of the state”.

And they do. Beijing’s corporate debt totals about 138pc of GDP, almost double the ratio in the US. But Chinese companies’ interest costs amount to less than 1pc of turnover, compared with 5pc for their American peers.

The effect of this fresh wave of cheap credit has been immediate.

China’s domination

Between 2021 and 2024, the number of products where China accounts for more than half of global exports nearly doubled, from 192 to 315.

China’s trade surplus will again surpass $1tn this year. The surplus with both Germany and France has doubled in the past year. For the EU as a whole, it amounts to more than €1bn (£840m) a day.

Although this export surge makes China appear like a rising economic superpower, the boom in cheap credit and factory exports has a dark side.

Companies are exporting their credit-fuelled output because Chinese households, burnt by the property crash, are not spending. At home, Chinese companies are forced into painful discounting wars just to move stock.

Profitability has plummeted and one in three companies is loss-making. Without the exports, which often provide more than 40pc of revenue, many businesses would be unviable.

Yet the banks keep lending and lending. Often, they have to discount the interest rate simply because otherwise the borrower would go bust.

Instead, it is European competitors who are absorbing the blow. In Britain, some have complained to the Trade Remedies Authority (TRA), which can impose quotas or tariffs.

The TRA has sought to protect local manufacturers from cut-price Chinese imports of everything from ceramics to ironing boards, tyres and cherry-pickers.

One recent TRA ruling noted that Chinese companies “have access to preferential financing, and access to financing from institutions which implement public policy objectives or otherwise do not act independently of the state”.

The TRA added: “They have more flexibility and can adjust their business and pricing strategies to maximise their export sales and gain market share in the UK, even if they would have otherwise made negative profit margins.”

No easy answers

Given that the Government is aware of the problem, many businesses want to see it push back harder. “There are probably plenty of stones that could be unturned,” one industry veteran says.

Rhodium’s Boullenois says the same is true in Europe, where Brussels’s trade directorate is overwhelmed with business requests for protection.

“We’re protecting too few products. Our defences need to be much broader, and work much faster,” she says.

But if the EU and US protect their own markets, more of the ultra-cheap Chinese exports will simply shift to Asia, Africa and Latin America – displacing European and American rivals in those countries’ markets.

“We normally look at how much is China selling to the EU. A lot less time is spent thinking about how many EU products the Chinese manufacturers are displacing in foreign markets – and it’s huge,” says Joe Peissel, of the consultancy Trivium China.

The battle against China’s factories is on in earnest. But as long as the Chinese are backed up by the bazooka of the country’s banking system, it will be a war that the West will struggle to win.

data.title: British baked beans ‘under threat from Burnham tariffs’
data.description:
British baked beans are under threat from Andy Burnham’s decision to cut tariffs on imported food, manufacturers have warned.

On Tuesday, the Government announced the suspension of tariffs on more than 100 food products, including cutting the 16 per cent levy on tinned beans.

The move was part of a package of measures the Chancellor announced in his Budget to give families “breathing space” amid the cost of living crisis.

However, British food bosses have warned that cheap exports from the US and China could undermine the country’s major bean processing industry.

The Heinz baked bean plant in Wigan, Greater Manchester, employs up to 850 people and produces 1.5 million tins a day. The Princes Group, which makes Branston baked beans, is owned by Italian food conglomerate Newlat and is one of Britain’s biggest food manufacturers with around 2,000 UK staff.

Karen Betts, chief executive of the Food and Drink Federation (FDF), said Mr Healey’s Budget had done “nothing to ease the pressures food and drink manufacturers are under”.

“One of the Chancellor’s flagship announcements, removing tariffs from some food and drink products, will have no meaningful impact on consumer prices,” she said.

“But it will undermine British factories and their workers, grappling with much higher costs, producing the same products.”

A spokesman for the Princes Group said: “Based on our understanding of the proposals so far, removing tariffs on imported finished baked beans is unlikely to have a meaningful impact on prices, particularly as there are currently no tariffs on the imported haricot beans used by UK manufacturers and no tariffs on EU imports.

“We believe measures that help address the higher costs of manufacturing food in the UK, particularly energy costs, would have a greater impact for both consumers and British businesses.”

The tariff announcement was made days after the Prime Minister said he would put the British family favourite in his emergency box in case of a national disaster. Asked what items he would stockpile, he picked baked beans, soup and Twiglets.

The FDF said it was also concerned about the lifting of tariffs on boiled sweets, toffees and caramels and pressed sweets like Love Hearts and Parma Violets, as well as chocolate.

Last year, the UK and US both applied a tariff of up to a 10 per cent on chocolate imports from the other country. Since then, the US has increased its tariff to 20 per cent and the UK has just removed it for most products.

In addition, the FDF said there were concerns around jams, marmalades and purees, tomato ketchup, tomato sauces, soups and broths.

“Food and drink manufacturing should be central to the Government’s growth and reindustrialisation agenda,” said Ms Betts. “But time and again, we are treated as an afterthought.

“The Treasury, in particular, has persistently failed to recognise the importance of food and drink manufacturing to jobs and prosperity across the length and breadth of the UK.”

The FDF said that particular companies that could be affected, including confectioners Nestle in York and Halifax, Haribo in Bradford, and Cadbury in Bourneville and Tiptree jam in Colchester.

The Government says the tariff suspensions, taken together with others announced earlier this year, will reduce consumer costs by up to £595m a year, saving households up to £21 on their annual food shop.

In its response to a consultation on the changes, the Government said it recognised there “may be some limited impacts on domestic producers of goods”, but said it “considers the benefits of this to consumers, through reduced costs, outweigh those risks”.

data.title: Landlords return to London as flat prices plunge
data.description:
Buy-to-let investors are starting to come back to London as flat prices plunge and rental yields rise sharply.

A combination of soaring rents and discounted purchase prices means landlords are buying flats in the capital at the fastest pace in years.

The share of London-based investors purchasing in the city has jumped from 34pc last year to an 11-year high of 39pc, according to Hamptons.

Guy Gittins, the chief executive of Foxtons, London’s biggest estate agent, said: “What we’ve seen in the last three months is that because of the capital sums that we’ve seen coming down, particularly on taller blocks, we have started to see the return of the rental investor in quite interesting numbers.”

Mr Gittins added: “I was in our Canary Wharf office four weeks ago and we went through the seven agreed sales that week. Five of them were to rental investors. I hadn’t seen that for the last seven years in London.”

Analysis by Hamptons shows gross rental yields on newly purchased London flats have soared to 7pc, up from 6pc last year and the highest level on record since Hamptons’ dataset began in 2015.

The share of landlord buyers getting 10pc yields on flats has more than doubled, rising from 7pc in 2025 to 15pc this year. It is the first time the proportion has been in double digits since at least 2015. Five years ago the share was just 1pc.

Aneisha Beveridge, the research director at Hamptons, said: “Higher yields seem to be tempting some investors back into parts of the London market, particularly where prices have adjusted but rents remain strong.”

The numbers suggest the Government’s buy-to-let crackdown – which began in 2016 with the introduction of a three-percentage-point stamp duty surcharge on additional properties, and has ramped up recently with Labour’s Renters’ Rights Act and John Healey’s Budget increase in tax rates on rental income – is starting to backfire in the capital.

Investors have been selling up for years, driving a shortage of supply that has sent rents soaring and triggered pain for the renters many of Labour’s policies were intended to help.

Now, investors are returning to the market to profit from the high rents, which continue to rise.

Office for National Statistics data show monthly rents in London in October were up by 3.7pc year-on-year and had soared by 31.2pc since the same month in 2022.

In contrast, prices of London flats, which is the market where buy-to-let investment is typically concentrated, were down by 6.3pc year-on-year in September, according to Land Registry figures. They have fallen by 10.6pc since their last peak in August 2022.

Falls are even steeper in the capital’s inner boroughs, where flat prices were down by 8.5pc year-on-year in September and have fallen by 12.6pc since their 2022 peak.

Adam Jennings, the head of residential at Chestertons, said: “Internally, we are starting to see property prices have got to a level where it is actually attractive from a yield perspective for investors to reinvest. Rents are high, prices are low.”

Mr Gittins added: “For the first time in my property career, we can sell a property to a rental investor with an 8pc, 9pc or 10pc yield in pretty much every regional patch [of London] – in central, north, south, east and west.

“When I was an estate agent selling properties for the first 10 years of my career in central London, I never sold a single property to a rental investor with more than a 3pc yield.”

data.title: Veterans forced to take 5am rail replacement bus to Remembrance Sunday
data.description:
Veterans have been offered a rail replacement bus at nearly 5am to reach Remembrance Sunday events in London.

Major Christopher McLean, 67, from Wiltshire, said the arrangements were “not good enough” and would prevent fellow veterans attending memorials.

In an email seen by The Telegraph, the Royal British Legion warned Cenotaph Parade ticket-holders that rail engineering works would bring disruption on Nov 8.

The charity advised veterans that South Western Railway and Network Rail Wessex were offering limited one-way bus travel from Winchester and Salisbury railway stations that were departing at 4.45am to arrive at London Waterloo at 8am.

Scheduled replacement bus services are also operating, requiring changes between rail and bus services to arrive in London on time.

Major McLean, who lives outside Salisbury, told The Telegraph that the disruption meant he would have to get up at 3.45am, which was not ideal at his age.

“No one seems to have thought this through,” he told The Telegraph, adding: “If I had planned like that in my Army logistics career, I would have been sacked.”

Veterans forced to ‘make other arrangements’

Major McLean said that veterans would be prevented attending events in the capital because of the disruption.

He said: “Lots of us are in our 70s. What about the implications for people who are infirm? It’s not good enough. Most of the guys I know are going to have to make other arrangements.

“Luckily, I can go up the night before and stay with relatives in Surrey. If I hadn’t had family there, I would have pulled out.

“Others are looking at paying for two nights in a London hotel, which is expensive. The Royal British Legion does a great job getting this all together, but the wider logistics haven’t been considered properly.”

Veterans would have been able to leave closer to 7am if the trains were running. This would still have allowed them enough time to arrive in Whitehall, pass through police security procedures and form up on the Cenotaph for 10.30am.

Major McLean said the rail disruption was the latest woe to be bestowed on veterans.

He said: “Prosecutions of veterans, underfunding of defence – it’s one thing after another, which is really upsetting this community. This is the latest mark of disrespect.”

Veteran’s fiercely oppose Labour’s Northern Ireland Troubles Bill, which is currently in the House of Lords, arguing that it does not adequately protect former service members.

Col Richard Kemp, a retired British Army officer who served from 1977 to 2006, criticised the lack of foresight by the railway operators.

“This is probably the most important day of the year when people can come together and pay respects to the war dead,” he said, adding: “It should be given priority above other events.

“Veterans should be treated with the utmost respect, including by the railway companies. This clearly isn’t good enough.”

Last month, the Government announced that it was extending free railway travel on Remembrance weekend, which currently covers serving military staff, veterans and one next of kin of a service-person who died while serving.

However, networks across the country will be disrupted by engineering work on Nov 7 and 8.

South Western Railway, the first operator to be renationalised by Labour in May 2025, apologised to veterans whose journeys would be affected.

A spokesman said: “South Western Railway is proud of its commitment to the Armed Forces community and this year received the Ministry of Defence Gold Award.

“Unfortunately, long-planned and essential engineering works this weekend mean veterans will need to use a combination of train and rail replacement services to travel to London Waterloo.

“We investigated whether the engineering works could be rescheduled, but this would have meant deferring essential track maintenance to maintain the long-term safety and reliability of the railway.”

A spokesman for the Royal British Legion said: “We’ve worked with the rail authorities to contact veterans affected by planned engineering works so they know a rail replacement service has been arranged.”

data.title: Twelve flights diverted across Europe after bomb threats
data.description:
Twelve flights have been diverted across Europe following a series of bomb threats.

Thursday’s disruption comes days after similar incidents in which eight planes, including three from the UK, were grounded over what Britain dismissed as a “malicious hoax”.

Three of Thursday’s incidents involved flights bound for Italy.

An Aer Lingus flight from Dublin to Rome was diverted to Normandy following a bomb alert, the French prime minister’s office said.

The office of Sébastien Lecornu, the French prime minister, said all 151 passengers and six crew members were safe, and that military bomb defusal teams were examining the plane.

A Finnair flight bound for Helsinki landed in Rome after a threat was reported on board, while a Wizz Air service from Milan Malpensa to Warsaw was diverted to Vienna.

A Polish Airlines flight from Warsaw to Brussels landed at Zaventem airport in Belgium after the crew received a “suspicious report concerning a flight to Brussels airport”.

Three more aircraft were forced to land at airports in Bulgaria following bomb threats. 

Two of the planes – travelling from Copenhagen and Madrid respectively – landed in Sofia, the broadcaster bTV, citing the interior minister, reported.

A third aircraft, flying from London, landed in Plovdiv, according to reports. Four planes flying to Prague had been the subject of bomb threats and were preparing to land, according to Czech police. 

A Wizz Air flight from Milan to Bucharest was also targeted, Romanian intelligence services said.

On Thursday morning, Spanish authorities said three flights at Madrid were affected by hoax threats.

None of the threats reported this week have been found to be genuine, despite triggering dozens of unplanned landings as well and escorts by fighter jets.

The EU’s transport commissioner said it was “too early to draw conclusions” on whether Thursday’s spate of bomb threats were linked.

Apostolos Tzitzikostas said in a message posted on LinkedIn that he had asked EU security authorities “to cooperate closely with airport operators, airlines and law enforcement authorities” over the bomb threats.

On Tuesday, at least seven planes were subjected to threats. A flight to Sofia was similarly affected on Monday.

An airport in Warsaw was briefly shut and the Italian air force accompanied one of the flights to Rome. An Israel-bound cruise ship was also searched for bombs in Greece.

A British Government spokesman told The Telegraph that the threats against the UK flights had been a “malicious hoax”, though it was not clear how they had been orchestrated.

Speculation quickly centred on Moscow, with a former MI6 intelligence officer telling The Telegraph that it was his first thought when he learned of the bomb threats, which he said fitted “a pattern of behaviour” by the Kremlin.

The flight disruption follows a week of chaos, with dozens of supermarket fridges across Europe hacked on Monday. The attacks caused large amounts of food to spoil after hackers gained remote access to in-store fridge units and turned up their temperatures, in some cases to as much as 80C.

Hackers also targeted France’s national blood bank, raising the temperature of its cold storage rooms to boiling point.

Facilities at Coolworld were heated to 110C overnight on Sunday after hackers gained access to the temperature settings remotely, Le Canard enchaîné reported. The rooms are normally kept at -30C to preserve donor blood samples.

An on-duty technician detected the unusual rise in temperatures. France’s health ministry said there had been no consequences for patients and no plasma had been destroyed.

The Kremlin said European media accusations of Russian involvement in ‌cyber attacks on supermarkets were not backed up by any evidence.

Dmitry ⁠Peskov, a Kremlin spokesman, told reporters on Thursday: “These are absurd claims. As always, they are backed up by absolutely ‌no reasoning, no evidence whatsoever, and yet here we have ⁠such ⁠baseless accusations against our country, implicating it in everything.”

However, pro-Russian hackers have claimed responsibility for the cyber attacks on fridges.

The pro-Russian hacking collective NoName057(16) claimed to have worked with Z-Pentest, another pro-Russian hacker group, to launch the attack.

A video claiming responsibility for the attack was posted on Telegram, according to the Danish media outlet DR.

In the video, titled Operation Chronicle: Danfoss, the hackers claimed to have “dealt a crushing blow to Danfoss and Dixell XWEB equipment”.

Danfoss and Dixell XWEB were the refrigeration companies targeted in the cyber attack.

“We didn’t even need malware for that. We just exploited the systems’ built-in features,” the hackers said.
