data.title: ‘Tesla of China’ could make cars in Britain as Burnham considers tariffs
data.description:
A company nicknamed the “Tesla of China” is considering manufacturing its vehicles in Britain as Andy Burnham mulls tariffs on Beijing’s electric car companies.

Brian Gu, the vice-chairman and president of Xpeng, told The Telegraph it would be “natural to think about local manufacturing” if sales in Britain hit a certain level.

The comments came as the Guangzhou-headquartered company this week announced plans to launch five new luxury vehicles aimed at British buyers.

Xpeng has been seen as a potential challenger to Tesla, pursuing a similar strategy of hi-tech vehicles packed with self-driving technology, while it has also developed humanoid robots.

Its sleek coupes, such as the LO3, share similarities with Tesla’s vehicles, pitting the Chinese companies directly against Elon Musk’s car business.

At a launch at the luxury Fairmont Windsor Park Hotel on Thursday, Xpeng unveiled the UK version of its LO3 SUV coupe, which it said would start at £32,990 and feature a range of more than 300 miles.

Speaking to The Telegraph, Mr Gu said the company would consider building vehicles in Britain if its launch in the market is a success.

Mr Gu said: “It depends on the success that we anticipate from these launches. We hope to generate a substantial business. And once we reach a certain volume, then it’s natural to think about local manufacturing.”

It comes as the Prime Minister considers imposing tariffs on Chinese electric cars. The EU has already enforced steep tariffs of up to 35.3pc on Chinese electric vehicles (EVs) and the Prime Minister has been seeking closer ties with Europe, raising the prospect the UK will adopt similar rules.

Jonathan Reynolds, the Business Secretary, has been drafting a tariff blueprint and Anas Sarwar, the trade minister, said last month that Britain and the EU must “work together and act in lockstep” to combat the flood of Chinese EV imports.

Xpeng’s latest UK vehicles will be built in China and shipped to Britain, meaning they would fall foul of any prospective tariff regime. It also produces cars for Europe out of a factory in Austria, although this plant is already near full capacity.

Xpeng’s launch in Britain follows a flood of other Chinese car brands that have swept across the UK market. The Jaecoo 7, made by China’s Chery, was the UK’s top-selling car in September, while BYD, which makes electric cars such as the Seal, has claimed close to 10pc of EV and hybrid sales so far this year.

The European tariffs have prompted Chinese carmakers to shift more production into the bloc to avoid the levies.

Some are also now exploring similar arrangements in the UK in anticipation of potential tariffs here. Chery, whose Jaecoo 7 is known as the “Temu Range Rover” for its lookalike appearance of the British marque, has sealed a deal with Nissan to explore making its cars in Sunderland.

Mr Gu said Chery’s deal was “very much a validation of their success in the UK market”. “If you want to be a leading player, you have to have more local capabilities,” he said.

The Xpeng boss said the company would have to “react” to any new UK rules on Chinese imports. It previously began making cars with Austrian manufacturer Magna in 2025 after Europe brought in its own tough levies.

Mr Gu said: “We have to react to whatever arrangement or regime there is, just like when we reacted to Europe when they announced EV tariffs on Chinese brands.

“We want to keep the current open, friendly and conductive market environment. But we as a company need to react whenever there is change.”

Xpeng plans to build a network of 100 retail outlets and service stations across the UK by the end of 2027. It is planning to open three flagship stores in London and Manchester in the next six months.

The company also announced plans to explore bringing its robotaxi service, known as Yoyo, to UK roads. “London is a very important, key robotaxi market. We also want to see how Yoyo can be tested,” Mr Gu said.

data.title: How we created a contemporary hobbit home
data.description:
When Gail Pirkis and her husband David spent two years scouring Wiltshire, Dorset, Somerset and Devon for the perfect site, and a house they could demolish and rebuild, they finally found what they were looking for on the edge of Dartmoor: a modest 1930s prefabricated bungalow with an extraordinary view. Now in its place is one of Britain’s most thoughtful contemporary country homes: a grass-roofed, granite-clad house that appears to grow from the landscape itself.

“The minute we saw the site on a beautiful May morning, we knew it was what we wanted. In fact, we bought the house without looking inside it,” recalls Gail, co-editor of the literary quarterly Slightly Foxed. The condition of the existing building was of little consequence; it was the setting that mattered. “It had the sense of being in its own private valley with a wonderful view overlooking both cultivated land and wilderness,” she says.

Gail imagined sheltered land, while David wanted a view and plenty of sky. With hills rising behind the house to protect it from the prevailing westerlies, and the land falling away in front before rising again in the distance, the site offered both. Living in London at the time, they were already thinking about a future in the countryside. “I think we always knew that we would like to end up living rurally, and we wanted a chance to build a house that would still be standing in several hundred years’ time,” she says.

For Gail, the move was also about creating somewhere conducive to her work. “I wanted to live somewhere quiet in which to edit, commission articles, plan which books we might reissue and think about long-term plans for the magazine. Our London office is a hive of activity, but not always the ideal place in which to think.”

Vision and design

Having bought the property in 1994, the couple initially submitted plans for an Arts and Crafts-style house, but their application was rejected by Dartmoor National Park. Undeterred, they appointed a new architect and took a different approach. “We planned a more timeless, contemporary house that would sit comfortably within the landscape and permission was granted.”

Their thinking was influenced by photographs of a house in Ireland that had been published in Perspectives, the then-Prince of Wales’s short-lived architectural magazine. Built into a slope and incorporating natural boulders at one end, the house provided a starting point for their own ideas. Working with architect Peter Hall, the couple developed a design shaped as much by the internal layout as by its relationship with the landscape. “We had a fairly clear idea of the layout we wanted inside, but it was Peter who gave external form to the internal layout,” explains Gail. “Crucially, he understood our wish that the house should feel part of the landscape.”

A key part of the vision was to create an uninterrupted connection between indoors and out. The gentle curve of the house is articulated through a series of right-angled corner windows, where the glass meets glass without the need for mastic or a supporting bar. “The corner windows give us the most glorious views,” says Gail. The result is a softened boundary between interior and landscape – an almost symbiotic relationship between the house and its surroundings.

Built into the hillside over two levels, the house has an unusual arrangement, with the upper storey set back from the floor below, creating what are effectively two ground floors. Every window opens directly onto meadow grass. Its boomerang-like curve changes orientation where the kitchen meets the hall, offering differing views from one end to the other. “We drew some inspiration from a Frank Lloyd Wright house in Manchester, New Hampshire, which has deep eaves and where the rooms flow into one another,” says Gail.

Both levels have green roofs: the lower is planted with crocuses, and the upper undulates like a meadow and is sown with wildflowers. Granite forms the exterior walls, while the windows, some sills and the undersides of the deep eaves are finished in oak.

Gail and David deliberately avoided fashionable features. “We didn’t want acres of glass and steel, and fittings that would soon date. Nor did we want an island in the kitchen, bar stools or a boiling tap,” Gail says. Although happy with the design, she admits that some decisions proved less successful. “We went for the cheapest quotation when choosing a builder and with hindsight the project would have been completed much faster and for the same amount of money had we gone for one of the higher initial quotes.”

Considering the environment

The choice of materials was largely guided by a desire to use local and reclaimed resources. The granite was sourced from the spoil heap of a disused quarry about 10 miles away, while oak from trees felled on the land was planked and seasoned for the outbuilding doors, porch bench and cupboards. Inside, the flooring is reclaimed oak and all the windows are double-glazed.

The house’s energy provision has also evolved. “Initially we had an oil-fired boiler and underfloor heating, but we switched to air source heat pumps about 15 years ago,” explains Gail. They’ve since added a wood burner to the kitchen. Their recent application to install solar panels behind an existing granite wall on the land was refused by Dartmoor National Park.

The landscaping was designed to complement the architecture while providing shelter from Dartmoor’s changeable weather. “Here, one needs protection, so the land around the house was landscaped to include existing granite boulders and a ha-ha that separates the garden area from the field below where sheep graze.” Beyond the house are fields, woodland, a small section of moor and tor and a restored lake. “We’ve planted 2,000 trees and now that these have matured, most local walkers don’t realise the house is here.”

Creating an interior for book lovers

With a burgeoning collection of books to accommodate, generous shelving was an essential part of the design. From a hallway flanked by green shelves – where grandchildren are fond of climbing up and down the two sets of library steps – to a staircase incorporating curved pigeonhole shelving, books are never far from reach. “The staircase was built off site before being dismantled and installed in the house, before which we enjoyed practising walking up and down, pausing at the shelves, imagining them in situ,” says Gail.

As Gail says: “Books really do furnish a house.” The collection now stands at 4,000. Alongside Slightly Foxed-published books such as a beautifully illustrated edition of Charles Phillipson’s Letters to Michael, Ysenda Maxtone Graham’s Love Divine and all the children’s books by Ronald Welch, Rosemary Sutcliff and BB (Denys Watkins-Pitchford) the publisher has reissued are David’s mountaineering books, a complete set of Everyman editions of PG Wodehouse, and Gail’s copies of Arthur Ransome’s books.

Just off the sitting room, an alcove serves as Gail’s home office. Lined with books – no surprise – it has a desk beneath a shallow dome with concealed lighting and a secret door leading to a small music room. “It’s a wonderful spot, somewhat inspired by Sir John Soane’s house in Lincoln’s Inn Fields, London.”

However, Gail doesn’t always stay at her desk. “I tend to migrate to the dining room for good light when checking proofs or to the kitchen table where the wood burner is going on colder days.” If she gets stuck on a difficult article, she heads outside. “I tend to go off to the veg patch to do a bit of weeding or take Stanley, our cocker spaniel, for a walk around the land. That usually clears the mind: this is the magic of living here.”

data.title: The renovation decisions that cause the biggest arguments (and how to avoid them)
data.description:
Renovating a property together should be a unique bonding experience, but anyone who’s ever bickered over a Farrow & Ball colour chart might understand why it can break even the strongest of relationships.

Alarmingly, a recent study by finance company Novuna found that almost one in five couples (19 per cent) seriously considered splitting up – or ended their relationship entirely – amid a home improvement project, while more than half (57 per cent) admitted to fighting over key decisions.

So why can a property makeover cause so much friction? “A home is not only our most expensive possession, but there’s huge emotional investment, too,” explains interior designer Piers Thurston. “Renovation choices are very subjective, and everyone’s vision is different. It’s also much more complicated than many realise, from red tape to liaising with trades, and costs that only emerge once work begins. People often sign up without really knowing what they’re getting into.”

For Valerie Couillard, a renovation project manager who is also trained in mediation, keeping the peace between clients is all in a day’s work. “My role is a bit like that of a couples’ counsellor,” she says. “It can get heated, but I use conflict resolution skills to make sure everyone is heard and brings their ideas to the table. The trick is to work out what really matters to each party and find solutions that tick as many boxes as possible.”

Here we reveal which décor dilemmas are most likely to spark full-scale domestic warfare – and how to navigate them without ending up in the divorce courts…

Paint colours

According to a 2025 study by Houzz, paint shades are the single biggest source of DIY discord, as cited by 51 per cent of respondents. “Colour is so personal,” says Couillard, who founded the Place Between to guide couples through challenging refurbs. “People often get cold feet about bold shades, but using mood boards and Pinterest can increase their confidence, or help them decide if the black ceiling one of them is keen on would look ridiculous or not.”

In moments of tension – or indeed, imminent marital collapse – she says there is usually a way through, with more daring shades reserved for smaller and less-prominent rooms. “Most people are willing to be flexible, so there’s usually a middle ground. With so many thousands of colour options, it doesn’t have to be a deal breaker.”

Thurston says he often looks beyond the paint itself. “I worked with a couple in Surrey on a TV snug, and while the husband preferred plain neutrals, his wife wanted more colour. To meet both their needs, we went for a very understated base colour, and created layering with different textures in subtle sage greens, which pulled in the colours of the beautiful countryside around them.”

Flooring

A close second in the Houzz study, 47 per cent of survey participants admitted clashing over the bewildering choice of carpeting, floorboards, stone and everything in between.

“Flooring is a real Pandora’s box,” says Couillard. “Clients may have their heart set on a type of tile, only to discover that excavation or other alterations are needed, which all add to the cost. There are also technical considerations like thickness, humidity and longevity.”

If squabbles arise, she says one solution is to identify what matters most to each partner and find a meeting point. “Hardwood floors are durable and easy to maintain, for example, but if the other person wants something cosier, you can add rugs.”

While a good designer will never try to sway a couple, Thurston says it is essential they warn them of potential pitfalls. “The most beautiful option is unfortunately not always the most practical,” he says. “If I point out issues like durability and maintenance, and whether someone wants to be sealing a natural stone floor every few years, opinions can change pretty quickly.”

Wall coverings

Wall materials caused rifts for 37 per cent of respondents in the Houzz study, showing that one person’s enthusiasm for flamboyant patterned wallpaper or elaborate tiling can be another’s design nightmare.

“Feature walls can look wonderful, but there’s a risk they’ll end up looking dated,” Thurston says. “I always recommend leaning towards who actually uses the room most, so for instance, if we’re looking at the kitchen, who does most of the cooking or entertaining? It’s really worth considering what the space is used for.”

Couillard says most bust-ups can be avoided if three-dimensional visualisation software is used. “It lets you see how a room would look with wallpaper on every wall, or just one,” she says. “If there’s disagreement over something like a botanical print, the answer might be to use it in a downstairs cloakroom. In my experience, the person who was originally unsure not only accepts it, but comes to love it.”

Appliances

With 22 per cent of couples confessing to feuds over appliances according to Houzz, gadgets such as bespoke wine fridges, built-in audio systems and integrated coffee machines can tip the already-frazzled over the edge.

“One partner is often far more interested in luxury appliances,” says Couillard. “If they really have their heart set on something, let them run with it – the other person can have final say on something else.” She adds that tussles over eye-watering price tags can be averted with a little forward planning. “I always start by asking for a wish list of everything they want if money was no object,” she says. “We work through that and gradually make compromises.”

Thurston agrees that determining which extras are non-negotiable before work begins is vital to prevent future hostilities. “Identify these things early, because when you get to the end of a project, there’s rarely any budget left.”

Worktops

When it comes to doing up a kitchen, few issues generate as much heat as the all-important worktop.

“Marble or natural stone can look amazing, but you have to factor in things like staining and sealing,” says Thurston. “I advise clients to consider overall kitchen design, which means getting samples and looking at them against the rest of the cabinetry, hardware, flooring and even the windows. A lot of the time, any issues are resolved based on what works with the rest of the scheme.”

In her role as a project mediator, Couillard believes in being armed with practical questions: “Who is cooking? Will you want to put hot pans on a wooden counter top, and what’s the risk of burning it?” she says. “I’ll also ask clients if they really want to replace existing marble or granite tops. Changing the cupboard fronts instead can save a lot of money and unnecessary waste,” she says.

Lighting

Even basic decisions over lighting can trigger flashpoints, which Thurston tackles with good old-fashioned compromise. “I’m working with a couple on a country house in Hampshire, and though the husband loves high-tech LEDs, his wife wants a more traditional feel,” he says. “So we’ve incorporated discreet LEDs into Shaker-style joinery around the fireplace and TV that give the look he wants, but still feel appropriate for the property.”

Battles over one-of-a-kind statement lights can be trickier to solve, however. “I’ve had a case where one person wanted a glamorous glass chandelier like you might see in a hotel, but their partner was quite bohemian and very against it,” says Couillard. “So we went for a big rattan pendant instead. That still looks great without being as blingy.”

Budgets

Finally, the thorny issue of money lies at the core of many renovation projects – backed up by Houzz’s findings that 37 per cent of couples lock horns over budgets.

“Usually clients take on good cop, bad cop roles,” says Thurston. “One wants to splash out, while the other is more insistent there’s a finite amount of money.” His solution is a high/low approach. “Some things are absolutely worth the investment, like a sofa which is a strong focal point. But we balance that by going for more cost-effective furniture elsewhere, like in a guest room which isn’t used as much.”

He advocates a healthy contingency pot for unexpected costs, while Couillard – who suggests allowing up to 25 per cent – says extinguishing financial flare-ups is a crucial part of her job. “I bring money up a lot, even though it can be boring,” she admits. “Different levels of finish can mean huge variations in budget, and sometimes I have to ask, ‘Can you afford that?’ I don’t necessarily want the answer. I want them to ask themselves.”

And if those conversations turn ugly? “That’s where the therapy element comes in,” she says. “I take it as a compliment when couples argue in front of me, because they’re not waiting for me to leave before they have a row. They bring it to the table and we deal with it together.”

data.title: The world is facing a new credit crunch
data.description:
High above the streets of Los Angeles, residents of the Beaudry can gaze across the Hollywood skyline, take a dip in a heated saltwater pool, practise their swing on a golf simulator and even send their dog to the spa.

Living in the 64-storey skyscraper doesn’t come cheap. Its 785 apartments command average rents of $4,200 (£3,200) a month, and 95pc are occupied.

By most measures, the $600m building sounds like a property developer’s dream. So why did its owner choose to hand back the keys?

Brookfield, the Canadian asset management giant that built the tower, decided last month that walking away made more sense than refinancing the $360m loan attached to it.

The company said the decision reflected the “entrenched market challenges” facing a city where property values had failed to rebound as strongly as expected. The pandemic hit Los Angeles particularly hard. Office vacancy rates remain roughly double what they were before Covid struck.

But the Beaudry’s troubles offer a cautionary tale about a global financial system being tested to its limits.

The tower is one of the most high-profile casualties of what Larry Fink, the high priest of global finance and boss of BlackRock, has called “the biggest competition for capital I have seen in 50 years in finance”.

For almost two decades, money was cheap. In the wake of the 2008 financial crisis and the credit crunch it triggered, central banks around the world cut interest rates close to – or sometimes below – zero. Easy borrowing kept economies afloat.

But in recent years that reality has been shattered. Inflation has come roaring back after multiple energy shocks and wars, sending interest rates soaring. At the same time, governments have borrowed heavily to fund ballooning liabilities following the pandemic. Add into the pot AI companies spending historic sums, and you have a dangerous cocktail.

“Governments across the developed world are running huge deficits,” Fink warned last month. “That borrowing is now colliding with tremendous demand from the private sector, much of it from technology companies.”

Today, a new credit crunch is setting in. Unlike the global financial crisis, when lending markets effectively froze up, money is still available.

But there is a growing divide between those who can still borrow at affordable rates and those struggling to borrow at all.

The consequences are being felt far beyond financial markets. In Britain, Landsec, one of the country’s biggest property companies, has shelved a £1.5bn redevelopment of Lewisham Shopping Centre in south-east London that would have delivered more than 1,700 homes.

Meanwhile, British Land has paused the next phase of its vast Canada Water regeneration project in Rotherhithe, south London, which was originally expected to deliver 4,000 new homes.

These are far from isolated examples. Across London, at least 42,000 homes have effectively been priced out of the development pipeline, including 12,000 affordable properties, according to analysis by Savills.

Companies are cutting jobs as their debt interest bills rise, and some are teetering on the brink.

The drama is playing out in slow motion, spread over years as companies, households and governments come to refinance loans and face much higher costs than the rock-bottom rates they enjoyed.

We may be at the beginning of this financial squeeze. The question is, how bad could it become?

Debt clock is ticking

Nearly 5,500 miles away from the Beaudry, another debt drama is playing out in Britain.

After almost three years of financial limbo, a decision on the future of debt-laden Thames Water may finally be in sight.

Britain’s biggest utility, which serves 16 million customers, stumbled into crisis after running up debts of around £13bn by 2020. As interest rates have jumped, that debt pile has soared to around £20bn.

The company’s creditors are putting the finishing touches to a “last and final” rescue bid for the stricken utility, after a previous proposal was rejected by ministers in June.

The lenders – a consortium of more than 100 financial institutions from across the globe – hope to persuade a Prime Minister who has pledged greater public control of utilities to give his blessing to the deal.

But sources said time was running out.

Some creditors are increasingly reluctant to provide fresh capital for Thames to meet its day-to-day spending commitments while so much political and regulatory uncertainty hangs over deliberations.

Others are considering walking away altogether and putting their money to work in situations with far less risk, according to another person close to the negotiations. Pimco, the $2tn American bond behemoth, had to be persuaded to stay on board, sources said.

The challenge for financially stretched companies such as Thames is that lenders can increasingly find safer and more attractive opportunities elsewhere.

“There is an ever-growing, unprecedented level of debt financing requirements, so debt investors are asking themselves: ‘I can either put my money into the AI rollout or into water, offshore wind farms or other forms of infrastructure’,” a City source said.

It is an extraordinary choice. Investors are weighing up whether to finance the pipes delivering water to millions of British homes or the data centres powering the AI revolution.

Unlike Thames and other debt-laden utilities whose credit ratings have long languished deep in junk territory, companies such as Meta and Microsoft retain strong investment-grade credit ratings despite enormous spending on AI infrastructure.

The sums involved are staggering. America is on course to pour more than $10tn into AI between 2025 and the start of the next decade, according to the Brookings Institution, a think tank.

As a share of the economy, the outlay will dwarf even the railway and telecoms booms of the past.

Despite growing concerns about the sheer level of borrowing taking place to bankroll the AI race, “much of this debt is being issued by companies with low leverage and rising earnings, meaning they’re well-positioned to support that debt”, JP Morgan’s private banking arm said in a recent note to clients.

Alongside AI companies, governments are the other group borrowing as if there were no tomorrow. Institute for International Finance data show that since the pandemic, global public debt has climbed by $40tn to $110tn.

Governments ripped up their fiscal rulebooks and brought out their chequebooks to shield businesses and households from economic calamity.

Now, demographic pressures are also increasingly weighing on government spending. As Andrew Bailey, the Bank of England Governor, recently highlighted, public expectations of bailouts may not yet have “adjusted back” to pre-lockdown norms.

All of this is making life harder elsewhere.

JP Morgan’s Jamie Dimon, the longest-serving bank chief executive in America, has warned that soaring government borrowing costs and spending on the AI boom risk spilling over into the corporate debt markets, pushing up financing costs for companies everywhere.

“There will be a point where the market will ask for more and more and more, and at one point that’ll feed into corporate debt, corporate credit spreads and things like that,” Dimon said.

In a scramble to avoid a crunch, many companies have been “very aggressive” at reducing borrowings after interest rate rises following the pandemic and then Russia’s war in Ukraine, says Luke Reeve, the head of debt advisory at EY.

But thousands of companies face a day of reckoning. Companies around the world are sitting on a $26.4tn pile of debt, according to S&P Global Ratings, with $13tn needing to be refinanced in the next five years.

In Britain, close to £85bn of corporate debt is set to mature in 2027 alone, according to estimates from EY. Of that, £27.5bn is in the form of bank loans and £57.2bn is owed to the bond markets.

For most, this so-called “refinancing wall” will manifest itself as a sharp rise in borrowing costs.

Even those that moved early have paid a steep price. In 2024, Ocado partially refinanced £500m of debt and saw its interest rate jump from 3.9pc to 10.5pc. The online grocer has since laid off hundreds of staff as it grapples with pressure to cut costs.

For the weakest companies, however, the problem is not simply that borrowing has become more expensive.

It is that investors may refuse to lend altogether.

“Too many businesses have extended and pretended because of the cheap capital,” says Arif Husain, the chief investment officer and head of global fixed income at T Rowe Price.

“We’re going to see a lot more differentiation between good and bad businesses going forward.”

Pressure is already starting to show at the bottom of the market. Interest rates charged on “the worst of junk bonds” are the highest they have been for years, says Husain.

“For the worst companies, that is being reflected in their borrowing costs right now.”

Healthcare, technology and media are the most vulnerable sectors to debt crises, according to S&P.

The scale of the challenges is daunting; companies at greater risk of default have to roll over $61.2bn of debt in 2027, a figure set to rise to $222bn in 2028.

Will they be able to?

“Strong, cash-rich companies can still borrow easily, just at higher rates,” Stephanie von Friedeburg, a senior banker at Citi, told an audience at the International Monetary Fund meetings in Bangkok last month.

“But lower-rated and leveraged companies face a tough refinancing wave that will test their business model.”

A shake-out is already under way.

More than $5bn of debt deals were shelved across the US and Europe last month amid struggles to borrow, according to Bloomberg.

A total of seven companies pulled fundraising plans in October, the biggest spate of postponements this year.

These include AVI-SPL, a Florida-based software firm, which abandoned attempts to raise $690m, and Mesirow Financial, a Chicago-based wealth manager, which put a $175m bond sale on ice.

In Europe, German energy outfit Iqony pulled a €550m (£460m) debt refinancing at the start of November amid subdued investor appetite, just days after a loan intended to finance a €2bn private equity-led takeover of French beauty and wellness brand Aroma-Zone was scrapped.

The borrowers may be very different, but the message from investors is increasingly the same: they are no longer prepared to finance every deal at any price.

And as companies struggle to find willing lenders, another major source of global capital is beginning to retreat.

For decades, oil-rich Gulf states were among the world’s most enthusiastic financiers, pouring their petrodollars into everything from luxury London hotels to American technology giants.

Now, Gulf money is turning inwards. As the Iran war piles pressure on government finances, those same sovereign wealth funds that helped to bankroll Western companies and infrastructure projects are increasingly being called upon to support their own economies.

BlackRock estimates that up to $100bn of Gulf capital could be redirected towards domestic investment in the near term.

Mounting costs to build

As the great wave of credit that washed across the world retreats, things are starting to come undone.

As Warren Buffett said: “You don’t find out who’s been swimming naked until the tide goes out.”

In the UK, the clearest signs of stress can be found in the property market. For many developers in London, the sums no longer add up.

Roughly 96pc of new homes in London are flats. The cost of building them has climbed by 60pc in the past decade, but their value has risen by just 10pc, according to Savills.

Berkeley Group, one of the country’s biggest builders, has said building homes in London is becoming impossible.

This is largely because of rising costs and red tape. Recent analysis by the Centre for Policy Studies warned that government rules had added up to £442,000 to the cost of a London home.

But soaring borrowing costs play a part too. Unaffordable mortgages are hitting demand. Higher mortgage rates are squeezing buyers, particularly those considering flats, and leaving developers uncertain whether they can sell properties at prices that justify the cost of construction.

Beyond property, signs of stress are emerging elsewhere. Virgin Media O2 (VMO2) this month outlined plans to cut thousands of jobs as it grapples with an escalating debt crisis.

The telecoms group is seeking to strip out £800m of costs per year amid growing concerns about its ability to service a £22bn debt pile.

VMO2’s bonds have slumped as investors baulk at the outlook for the company, which is facing fierce competition from broadband start-ups and uncertainty about its ability to buy up smaller rivals.

A record 738,144 UK businesses were in “significant” financial distress at the end of August, according to restructuring company Begbies Traynor.

It said many were “operating with limited financial headroom”. The firm has been producing its Red Flag report, which looks at the health of UK Plc, since 2004.

Spreading the risks everywhere

Even as rising borrowing costs put pressure on businesses, the debt-fuelled AI boom shows little sign of slowing down.

In the past 12 months, AI companies have received almost two thirds of US venture-capital dollars.

A quarter of US investment-grade debt issued this year has come from companies involved in AI, according to Goldman Sachs.

Yet there are cracks emerging there too, as some investors, such as New York City’s $325bn pension system, start turning down AI deals amid concerns about overexposure.

“You’ve really got to be in every asset class, and we are in every major economy on Earth. But now so much of that, sector by sector, market by market, is AI,” Mark Levine, the New York City comptroller, told Semafor, the US news platform.

It’s “a risk that we’re leery of”, said the city’s equivalent of a chief finance officer.

Tremors have begun to appear in the market, with shares and bonds of “neocloud” data centre companies falling sharply in recent weeks.

Governments, too, have faced warning shots that investors will not tolerate their gorging on debt forever. Bond yields have hit multi-decade highs across the West in a sign of unease. The International Monetary Fund has told countries to rein in borrowing urgently to avert a crisis – before it’s too late.

Not everyone will lose out in this new credit squeeze.

Rich investors may find themselves in an increasingly powerful position as companies compete for their cash. Many of those with money looking for a home for it will be “licking their lips”, says Reeve at EY.

For most of us, however, the consequences of a prolonged period of expensive borrowing could be far less welcome. Homeowners will come under pressure, debt-laden companies will cut jobs and governments will surely have to scale back spending, reducing public services in the process.

“Clearly, the people that will suffer most will be the ones that need to borrow the most,” says Husain at T Rowe Price. “The bigger mortgages – [more] higher leveraged consumers – will be most at risk here.”

A new financial world order is emerging, where money is increasingly flowing towards the strongest borrowers and away from those who need it most.

In the face of this new credit squeeze, even a skyscraper full of paying tenants is struggling.

data.title: How much cash should I have at home – and where should I keep it?
data.description:
The UK Government is urging households to stock up on basic supplies in case of emergencies such as cyber attacks, flooding, fire or power cuts.

Alongside practical items such as bottled water, a wind-up torch, a first aid kit and a portable power bank, the advice includes keeping some cash at home to provide essential backup if card payments or banking apps stop working.

Here, Telegraph Money explains how much cash is safe to keep at home, and the best way to store it.

  • Is it a good idea to keep cash at home?
  • How much cash is safe to keep at home?
  • Where should you store cash at home?
  • How else can I protect my access to money?

Is it a good idea to keep cash at home?

Although cash usage is on the decline in the UK, keeping a small amount of cash at home can be a practical safety net. Recent global events, from cyber attacks and data breaches to widespread power outages, have shown how quickly modern payment systems can break down.

Simon Phillips, a retail and foreign exchange business leader, said: “Most of us take card and contactless payments for granted, and the technology is great – right up until the moment it stops working.”

Last month, a Google system failure caused several banking apps to crash, which resulted in millions of Revolut customers being unable to access their money or use their bank cards, while users of Lloyds Bank, HSBC, Barclays, Bank of Scotland, Natwest, Halifax, Nationwide, Royal Mail and DPD also reported issues.

Keeping some cash at home can therefore be a sensible precaution to ensure you could still pay for essentials, such as food and fuel, in an emergency.

How much cash is safe to keep at home?

As a rule of thumb, you should have enough cash to cover essential spending for two to three days. For smaller households, this might be around £100, while larger households or those living in rural areas might prefer to keep up to £300 at home.

You might be tempted to keep even more, but Harriet Guevara, the chief savings officer at Nottingham Building Society, warned against going overboard.

“Beyond concerns like loss or theft, cash held outside the banking system loses any potential for interest, isn’t protected by the Financial Services Compensation Scheme (FSCS) and is often not covered in full by home insurance policies,” she said.

Most home insurance policies only cover cash up to a limit, usually between £200 and £500, so check your policy to be sure. Anything beyond that won’t be covered in the event of theft, fire or flood.

Sarah Coles, the head of personal finance at AJ Bell, also suggested having a broader backup plan.

She said: “If you’re worried about having access to your bank, it can make sense to have an arrangement with someone you are close to (and you trust) that you can call on in an emergency, and vice versa. In some cases, if you can’t withdraw money, you can still transfer it.”

Where should you store cash at home?

Cash at home should be kept securely. Yet research from security site Safe.co.uk found that more than two-thirds (67pc) of people keep valuables, including cash, in storage that is not locked.

Anthony Neary, the company’s security expert, said: “Far too often, people are relying on obvious hiding places, such as inside drawers or cupboards, or even out on shelves, which offer little to no protection against opportunistic theft.

“Instead, use a secure storage solution such as a compact home locker or cash box with a lock.”

Storage should be fireproof, as well as heavy or bolted to a wall so that it would be difficult to remove if someone broke into your home. It should also be stored out of sight, away from windows and doors, according to Vlatka Lake, of self-storage operator Space Station.

She said: “Lofts are ideal because they are hard to reach and sometimes require ladder access. If you do go for this option, make sure to store the cash in a sealed container to avoid it getting damaged or mouldy. It should be stored in a dry but well-ventilated area.”

Whatever you do, don’t keep your cash in a bedside drawer or under your pillows or mattress, as these are the first places intruders will check.

Ms Coles added: “There are some traditional hiding spots where burglars will look first, like the freezer, the sock drawer and biscuit tins, so they’re worth avoiding. If you have a lot of books, one option is to choose a book to hide it in. A burglar will run out of time looking for it.”

How else can I protect my access to money?

In addition to keeping some cash in hand, it may also be sensible to be prepared in case your bank experiences an outage.

Ms Coles said that some people will hold two current accounts for this reason, so that if one is inaccessible, they can still get hold of money deposited with a different bank.

Furthermore, the FSCS only guarantees your money up to £120,000 per person, per firm. So if your deposits are likely to go over the threshold, you should spread your money between accounts to ensure that you’re protected.

Similarly, it is considered good practice to keep some of your savings in an easy-access account so it is on hand in case of emergencies. However, this money will not generate the same level of interest as accounts that require notice, so it’s important to only keep what you need there.

data.title: British AI giant Nscale slows hiring in cost-cutting drive
data.description:
One of Britain’s biggest AI companies has put the brakes on hiring as it seeks to cut costs before a $35bn (£27bn) flotation.

Nscale has told executives to suspend recruitment in certain divisions and rein in spending amid a turbulent market sell-off, according to an email to staff seen by The Telegraph.

The intervention comes after breakneck growth at the company, one of a cluster of upstart data centre operators that have become the face of the AI spending boom.

The move comes as shares in AI and data centre companies slump and borrowing costs soar amid fears about the sustainability of the boom and after US voters turned against data centres.

Justin Osofsky, Nscale’s chief operating officer, told staff that the company was “pausing hiring for the next few months, with exceptions for critical roles, to give the business time to catch up with how quickly we’ve grown this year”.

He added that bosses would be “reducing discretionary spending across the company” and “holding ourselves to a higher bar for what we spend”.

The hiring slowdown is understood to relate to office functions, with the company still recruiting for roles building new data centres.

Nscale, which is backed by Nvidia, has grown from 300 employees earlier this year to more than 1,100. It warned in stock market filings earlier this month that it needed to raise more cash in the next year to fulfil signed deals.

Neoclouds such as Nscale have raised substantial sums of money to build data centres filled with high-end AI chips, hoping to rent them out to AI companies.

But the combination of rising interest rates, victories for anti-data centre candidates in this month’s US Midterms, and the departure of Jensen Huang, the Nvidia boss, have triggered a brutal downturn in neocloud shares.

Mr Huang was a key cheerleader of the movement, financing companies that in many cases were also his company’s own customers.

Nscale, founded two years ago by Josh Payne, an Australian former cryptocurrency executive, has raised more than $13bn and signed large deals with Anthropic and Microsoft.

Mr Osofsky, who recently joined from Meta, told staff: “Financing large projects is taking longer across the sector, and the companies that manage their cash and commitments carefully will be in the strongest position to capitalise on opportunities.

“Every dollar we preserve gives us more flexibility to fund our highest-priority projects,” he added. Rival companies have also said they need to get on top of costs.

Nscale said in September it had filed for a New York Stock Exchange initial public offering, reportedly at a valuation of up to $35bn. However, since then, shares in US rival CoreWeave have fallen by half, including an 11pc sell-off on Friday.

Nscale has also lost a $3.2bn deal with Microsoft to take space at its UK data centre because of delays securing a grid connection.

The company lost $1.7bn in the first nine months of this year on revenues of $308m.

The Telegraph can also disclose that Nscale warned Norwegian officials this month that its expansion plans in the country, where its flagship data centre is located in Loughton, Essex, could “fall apart” if a moratorium on new data centres is imposed.

Data centres across Europe are facing a political backlash amid concerns about their potential strain on power resources and grid connections.

In a letter sent to Norway’s energy ministry on Nov 1, seen by The Telegraph, Nscale called for an “urgent” meeting before the potential freeze. Days later, ministers confirmed a block on new grid connections and technical approvals for data centres until next August.

It is not clear which of Nscale’s projects are affected. Sites already approved are not affected by the Norwegian ban. But in the letter, Nscale says it has the “largest capacity reservations” in the country’s grid operator’s queue.

Nscale has a major data centre project in Glomfjord in the Arctic Circle, where its hydropower facility serves customers including China’s Bytedance. Construction work to expand the site has already been beset by delays.

The UK operator has also been linked to a series of other Norwegian projects that represent billions of pounds of investment.

The letter, from Nscale’s Norwegian government affairs chief, said: “We are currently in dialogue with most of the stakeholders considering large-scale new power generation in Norway ... These plans could quickly fall apart if a moratorium on the further development of AI centres in Norway is imposed.”

data.title: GSK plots £400m Cambridge research hub in push for cancer breakthrough
data.description:
GlaxoSmithKline (GSK) will invest £400m in a major new science hub in Cambridge as part of plans to pour more money into developing new cancer drugs.

The pharmaceuticals giant said it planned to acquire a new 300,000 sq ft site on the Cambridge Biomedical Campus, which will house most of its research and development (R&D).

The new centre of excellence will employ more than 1,000 scientists, GSK said, with its researchers developing new vaccines, HIV treatments and cancer drugs.

However, the move will also end the FTSE 100 company’s 50-year relationship with Stevenage, Hertfordshire, which was previously its main UK research base. Some Stevenage staff will be asked to relocate to another lab in nearby Ware.

The investment in Cambridge comes as GSK seeks to ramp up its pipeline of medicines under Luke Miels, its new chief executive, who took on the role from Dame Emma Walmsley at the start of the year.

The company has been accelerating investment in cancer drugs after it acquired US-based Nuvalent in June for nearly £8bn.

GSK won approval from US medical regulators last week for Jideytro, a lung cancer treatment secured as part of the takeover of Nuvalent.

The decision to open a new Cambridge campus will bolster the Government’s efforts to turn the 100-mile corridor between Oxford and Cambridge into an economic powerhouse.

GSK said the investment would build its presence “in the heart of the UK’s life sciences ‘Golden Triangle’” – made up of Oxford, Cambridge and London.

Earlier this year, Rachel Reeves, the former chancellor, set out Labour’s ambition to turn the area into a hub for science businesses, building new homes and transport links to create Europe’s “Silicon Valley”.

The Cambridge Biomedical Campus already employs more than 22,000 people and hosts treatments for one million patients each year. GSK hopes to build its links with research hospitals in Cambridge and benefit from proximity to the University of Cambridge.

Mr Miels said: “This investment will accelerate our R&D and help us deliver new, competitive products.”

On Tuesday, GSK also announced plans for a major cost-cutting drive aimed at saving £1.9bn by 2029 to fund the development of new drugs. The savings are expected to include job cuts around the world, including reducing some back-office roles.

Alongside the plans for a new Cambridge site, GSK said it had launched 20 phase three trials as part of its plans to expand its pipeline of treatments.

These trials are the final stage of clinical testing before a drug is submitted to the Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency for approval.

Andy Burnham, the Prime Minister, said the £400m investment was “a vote of confidence in British business”.

Life science is one of eight sectors that form part of the Government’s modern industrial strategy.

The investment from GSK comes after its rival AstraZeneca announced that it would pour £200m into its Cambridge site, along with £100m for a project in Macclesfield, Cheshire.

GSK’s relocation to the Cambridge Biomedical Campus means Britain’s two largest pharmaceutical companies will neighbour each other in the city. GSK said it would keep its global headquarters in London.

data.title: Ofgem launches urgent inquiry into power grid delays
data.description:
Britain’s energy watchdog has launched an urgent inquiry into plans to accelerate electricity grid connections after they inadvertently caused more delays.

Ofgem said on Thursday it would investigate why an overhaul designed to speed up access to the grid had instead made it harder to secure a connection.

Developers have complained about lengthy waits to have their sites hooked up to electricity, which has stalled the rollout of new factories and homes.

The regulator said it shared the “frustration” of developers, acknowledging the outcomes from its reforms were “not good enough”.

The National Energy System Operator had been tasked with weeding out so-called “zombie projects” from a queue of schemes waiting for a connection.

However, Ofgem said that “the majority of projects in the reformed queue are seeing delays rather than advancements”.

Akshay Kaul, the energy watchdog’s director-general for infrastructure, said that the connection dates offered to too many projects were “not good enough”.

“Our inquiry will establish transparently what has driven these delays,” he said.

The inquiry came as Labour moved to scrub all mention of its controversial 2030 green energy policy from an announcement hailing the latest round of net zero subsidies.

The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero on Thursday appeared to distance itself further from a target to run the UK’s electricity grid entirely on low-carbon technologies by the end of the decade.

Known as Clean Power 2030, the proposal was a centrepiece of Labour’s election manifesto and championed by Ed Miliband, who became energy secretary.

However, the policy appears to have been dropped from government communications after an announcement on new wind and solar farm subsidies omitted the reference.

It comes after Mr Miliband was moved to the Foreign Office this summer, replaced by Miatta Fahnbulleh as Energy Secretary.

His departure was quickly followed by that of Chris Stark, appointed by Mr Miliband to oversee the Clean Power 2030 programme.

Ministers still refer to “clean power”, but they set no date and are pledging to reform the system to focus on costs rather than timelines.

It follows warnings from John Healey, the Chancellor, that while he supported clean power “we will only buy projects that can lower bills while strengthening our energy security”.

Michael Shanks, the energy minister, has also said future clean power projects had to prioritise lower bills.

“These reforms … make the auction process more transparent and competitive, so we secure the best projects at the best price for consumers,” he said.

The shift in emphasis from decarbonisation by 2030 to cutting prices is likely to mean fewer applications or approvals for new renewables projects.

These have always been heavily reliant on subsidies in the form of Contracts for Difference.

However, the latest auction round set no effective budget for the subsidies, leaving developers uncertain of the funding.

data.title: Financier caught up in row with neighbours over basement golf simulator
data.description:
A financier has won planning permission to dig 4m under his driveway to build a golf simulator and games room, despite objections from neighbours.

Tim Woolford secured permission to install a basement below the drive of his modern home. The underground room will be 13ft 1in deep and have a simulator, bar area and pool table.

Neighbours in Winchester, Hampshire, where homes are worth an average of £1m, say they have environmental concerns about the project and that the works will affect their lives for months.

Residents have referred to Mr Woolford’s home as the “Lego house”, because of its striking modern design, and say it is not in keeping with traditional properties in the area.

Winchester City Council has approved the plans with conditions, despite a planning officer recommending it be refused.

Mr Woolford, his wife and their two children have lived in the house since the coronavirus pandemic and, in drawing up an underground extension, had sought to create an extension plan that would have the least impact on neighbours.

He said: “Our view was that we wanted to do something that would impact people the absolute least as possible. Some of the people that objected misunderstood what would be here when the builders were done.”

Mr Woolford, who is managing director of a finance-management company in London, said he and his wife would still be able to park on the driveway when the building work was completed, so this would not affect the on-street parking.

He said he wanted to build the space for his two sons, who are aged seven and eight, and wanted to install a golf simulator, because they were interested in the sport.

Mr Woolford said: “We have kids that are growing, and it is good for them. We didn’t actually think there would be any discussions about the plans. We did quite a few developments to the house a few years ago, and arguably this has been more contentious.”

He said one of his sons played the guitar and he thought it would be less disruptive to allow him to play in the basement extension – sometimes referred to as an iceberg basement.

Mr Woolford said: “People go into their lofts and convert garages, and I didn’t want to go into the loft and put big windows, and I don’t have a garage to convert.”

He said the process should be reasonably quick and should not cause very much disruption to the neighbours.

He said: “It is actually a quick build. The soil can be taken out within a week. We should be done in about 10 to 12 weeks, so much more minimal than people expect.”

Mr Woolford said the complaints were a “group effort” and they came from houses further down the street, who were not as affected by the works. As well as being 4m deep, the new basement will be 9.5m in width, and 10.9m in length.

Hazel Agombar, who has lived in the street for 20 years, said the house was already referred to as the “Lego house” and she did not think more work should be done to it.

She said: “I didn’t want it to set a precedent of people applying for basement extensions because of the disruption. We have people who are wheelchair users regularly using this street. There is limited parking up the top.

“This is a lovely street, people get on. It’s very green and leafy, and I just thought it was a poor reason to try to change the character of it and try to navigate that disruption.”

Mrs Agombar said that she thought the decision contravened the council’s local plan to make Winchester more environmentally friendly. She said: “It seems to go against the new local plan. It is only one development but it seems like it is starting a precedent. It is for a golf simulation room.

“This is crazy. They have this massive house with a cinema room and garden. If you want a bigger house, maybe you should move if you want to dig up a conservation area.

“The council has allowed a highly intensive carbon footprint development. Digging up that drive is going to be hugely carbon intensive.”

Another objector is Keith Hatter, 79, who is blind and has lived on the street for the last 14 years.

He said: “The main reason was that it involves digging out to about 2.5m of the ground in front of the house, and I am slightly worried that this might have an effect on the soil structure.”

Mr Hatter added: “The second objection I have come to second-hand – because I am totally blind – is that it might interfere with the character. It would involve the trees and general flora in front of the house being removed and have a slightly detrimental environmental effect.”

data.title: AstraZeneca dumped by investors over £300bn US merger talks
data.description:
AstraZeneca shares have taken an £18bn hit after investors baulked at reports it was plotting a mega-merger with a US rival.

Shares in Britain’s second-most valuable company slumped on Monday after it emerged that AstraZeneca had held talks about a potential $400bn (£300bn) tie-up with Bristol Myers Squibb.

If completed, the merger would create one of the world’s largest pharmaceutical businesses. The potential deal would also raise fears that AstraZeneca could shift its business to the US in a blow to Britain.

However, analysts said it was a high-risk deal that risked destroying more value than it created. It would be one of the biggest mergers of all time, meaning any missteps could prove hugely costly, and would be likely to draw the attention of competition regulators and politicians.

News of the talks, first reported by the Financial Times, sent AstraZeneca’s shares plunging 9pc on Monday to their lowest level since September 2025.

Markus Manns, a portfolio manager at Union Investment and an ‌AstraZeneca ⁠shareholder, told Reuters: “A combination with Bristol ​does not make strategic or financial sense.

“Many past mega-mergers have destroyed value and there is no apparent need for Astra to do it.”

Jefferies analysts said in a note: “If there is ​one company that doesn’t need financial engineering, it’s AstraZeneca.”

Michael Leuchten, an analyst at Jefferies, said he was “perplexed” by the potential takeover. He said investors backed the company because of its consistent sales growth, not because management “go out and do big deals”.

AstraZeneca is worth around £184bn on the London Stock Exchange, while New York-listed Bristol Myers Squibb has a market value of $133bn.

Bristol Myers Squibb shares surged as much as 3.8pc on Wall Street on Monday.

Analysts said competition concerns would be the biggest hurdle to a deal as both companies have large cancer treatment businesses.

The potential deal could also trigger a political backlash from Donald Trump’s administration, Jefferies warned.

Mr Leuchten added: “AstraZeneca would effectively be a UK-based acquirer of one of America’s large Pharmas, at a time when US policymakers are focused on domestic manufacturing and strategic industries.”

The deal would raise questions about AstraZeneca’s continued links to Britain as Sir Pascal Soriot, its chief executive, pushes ahead with a pivot towards the US.

AstraZeneca upgraded its listing on the New York Stock Exchange last September to let American investors buy its shares directly, while keeping its listing in London.

The move put AstraZeneca’s New York listing on a par with that of London, in what was seen as a blow to the UK’s struggling stock market.

AstraZeneca subsequently struck a $50bn deal with the Trump administration to invest in US manufacturing and transatlantic research facilities.

At the time, Sir Pascal described the drugmaker as a “very American company”.

The business subsequently agreed to sell some medicines at a discount to the US Medicaid programme to avoid being hit with tariffs.

Despite this, Britain’s biggest drugmaker has insisted that it intends to remain headquartered in Cambridge and retain its listing on the London Stock Exchange.

Mr Leuchten said buying Bristol Myers Squibb as a way to shift permanently to the US would be “a fairly drastic way to go about it”.

However, Neil Birrell, the chief investment officer at Premier Miton, an AstraZeneca shareholder, said the likelihood of the pharmaceutical business shifting its shares to the US would increase if the Bristol Myers Squibb deal went ahead.

Mr Birrell added: “There hasn’t been a huge amount that I’ve seen coming out from any of the authorities – whether it be the Government or the London Stock Exchange – of any great substance to try and keep these sort of companies here.”

The Prime Minister said the talks were “a private matter for the companies involved”.

A No 10 spokesman said: “More broadly, the UK life sciences sector is one of our greatest national assets, driving innovation, skilled employment and investment across the country while developing medicines that improve health outcomes and save lives.”

AstraZeneca has around 10,000 staff at five UK sites, including 4,000 at its main facilities in Cambridge and Macclesfield and another 2,000 in London and Luton.

Steve Boden, a regional organiser at GMB Union, said he was seeking urgent assurances from AstraZeneca that jobs would be protected.

“These reports of a merger are causing great concern amongst AstraZeneca’s loyal workers. While no deal has been formally announced, mergers can create pressure to cut costs, so staff are understandably worrying about what this could mean for them.”

The proposed mega-merger will evoke memories of Pfizer’s attempts to take over AstraZeneca a decade ago.

The US company’s acquisition ultimately collapsed after a wave of resistance from the board and politicians alike.

Ed Miliband, then Labour leader, said at the time that Pfizer’s assurances about protecting research and saving jobs were “worthless”.

Bristol Myers Squibb is headquartered in Princeton, New Jersey, and was started in 1858, making it one of the US’s oldest pharmaceutical companies.

data.title: Hundreds of pharmacies face closure from Labour tax raid
data.description:
Hundreds of pharmacies are facing closure because of soaring business rates, with owners warning that high taxes are forcing them to cut services for vulnerable patients.

Almost half of the 420 pharmacy owners surveyed by the National Pharmacy Association (NPA) said they were considering shutting down their practices because of higher business rates bills.

The trade body warned that pharmacies, many of which are family-run businesses, are unable to offset the higher tax burden by raising prices, which are fixed by the NHS.

The NPA found 55pc of pharmacy operators were considering moving to cheaper premises, raising fears that some rural and coastal communities could be left without a local branch.

Andy Burnham has made lowering business rates for high-street businesses a key pillar of his summer policy blitz, announcing a 20pc reduction for pubs, clubs and live music venues from April next year.

However, pharmacies have been excluded from the relief.

The tax squeeze has intensified since business rates were increased for many properties after Rachel Reeves’s second Budget. Bills have also been affected by the latest revaluation of commercial property.

GPs and NHS dentists, meanwhile, have their business rates reimbursed.

Pharmacies are particularly exposed because most of their income comes from the NHS, meaning they cannot simply raise prices to cover higher costs. Roughly 90pc of pharmacies’ income comes from the health service, the NPA said.

Onkar Singh, who runs 20 pharmacies across the Black Country, Staffordshire, Herefordshire and Worcestershire, has seen his business rates bill rise by roughly 20pc to 30pc in the past year. His total bill is now about £250,000.

He has closed two of his pharmacies in the past two years and reduced opening hours across virtually his entire estate. He has also been forced to cut back services, such as offering free medicine deliveries to elderly patients.

Mr Singh said: “The last three years have been the worst period in my 30 years of pharmacy.

“People are having to close a lifetime’s worth of work and effort, and having to close or reduce hours or dip into their pension pot just to keep going for their communities.”

The NPA survey found that 92pc of pharmacies said their rates bill was preventing them from investing in their workforce or renovations. Some pharmacists have warned that their bills have tripled.

Mr Singh said the impact was particularly painful because pharmacies were often being asked to fill gaps elsewhere in the NHS.

He said: “It is frustrating that pubs and restaurants get the headlines, but pharmacies are actually delivering care.

“The NHS accepted that pharmacy did an exceptional job, but in terms of funding and support with business rates we seem to be forgotten.”

The NPA said 44 pharmacies had already closed this year, leaving the national network at its smallest since 2006.

Nine in 10 council areas have lost at least one pharmacy since 2022.

Olivier Picard, the chairman of the trade group, said pharmacies should receive the same rates treatment as GPs and dentists, arguing that they provide an essential health service.

A government spokesperson said: “Pharmacies already benefit from our wider business rates reforms, including permanently lower multipliers and our £4.3bn package to support ratepayers – and the government has increased funding for the sector by £340m this year as part of our shift to bring care closer to home.”

data.title: Workers fear losing jobs over train delays, warn MPs
data.description:
Workers fear losing their jobs because rail services are regularly late, MPs have warned.

A spate of line closures and cancellations during the summer heatwaves made it impossible for thousands of commuters to arrive at the office on time.

MPs at a Westminster Hall debate said workers were increasingly fearful of the lack of reliable train connections and urged the Government to spend more on rail infrastructure to improve punctuality.

Charlotte Cane, the Liberal Democrat MP for Ely and East Cambridgeshire, said: “One [constituent] in particular has written to say that because their train has been so unreliable for getting to their job in London that their employer is now putting them under pressure.

“They are becoming an unreliable member of staff and their employer doesn’t know when they are going to turn up to work.

“They are also having to make up the time at the end of the day, which means they are getting home very late. It makes it a complete nightmare for them.”

Desperate to protect their jobs, some workers were now considering moving house to be closer to stations with more reliable services, MPs said.

Others are considering giving up well-paid positions in London and other major cities for less lucrative roles closer to home.

Among the worst-hit lines this summer was the route between King’s Cross and King’s Lynn via Cambridge and Ely, the later of which lies in Ms Cane’s constituency.

It suffered three months of disruption, including 900 cancellations after normally damp peat beneath the tracks dried out, leading the ground to become uneven.

James Wild, the Conservative MP for North West Norfolk, which includes King’s Lynn, said people from the town who worked in Cambridge and London had found the disruption intolerable.

He told The Telegraph: “I’ve had quite a number of constituents who have said they’re thinking of moving jobs. They’ve been in tears and incredibly stressed.

“One lady said her husband, who commutes and is self-employed, had been driven to depression and was having suicidal thoughts because he was worried that he wouldn’t be able to provide for his family. It’s pushing people to breaking point.”

Mr Wild said some commuters had opted to drive to Peterborough on the East Coast Main Line, or Norwich, which has trains to Liverpool Street – both an hour away by road – to be sure of getting to work.

He said there were concerns that with the line suffering heat-related disruption for the past two summers, people would stop viewing King’s Lynn as a viable commuter town, which could have a knock-on effect on house prices.

Mr Wild questioned Andy Burnham about the matter in September, when the Prime Minister said he would “convene a rail summit soon”.

Richard Foord, the Liberal Democrat MP for Honiton and Sidmouth, said commuters to cities beyond London had also been affected.

He said restrictions imposed between London Waterloo and the West Country had in one case led a dental hygienist to cancel her 9am appointments “indefinitely”.

Simon Lightwood, the minister for local transport, said he could not rule out further weather-related disruption.

He added that while speed restrictions and closures might be frustrating, the railway’s primary duty was to keep passengers safe.
